articles.title_orig: Second QDA Forum Focuses on Real-World Deployments And Progress of Quantum Computing
articles.title_zh: Second QDA Forum Focuses on Real-World Deployments And Progress of Quantum Computing
articles.content_orig:
PRESS RELEASE — The second international Quantum Datacenter Alliance (QDA) Forum highlighted the progress towards commercial deployments and acceleration of distributed quantum computing architectures, while also outlining the next critical areas of focus for progress.
At the iconic Battersea Power Station, London, the QDA brought together technical, business, and government leaders to address one of the most pressing technical and ecosystem challenges: how to integrate emerging quantum hardware into existing and future data center infrastructure.
The agenda explored how quantum systems are moving from lab-scale demonstrations toward commercial deployment, highlighting that system level architecture, control, error correction, interoperability and power consumption have become as critical as the qubits themselves. Attendees also emphasised the importance of open sharing, interoperability, and collective thinking about the direction and future uses of quantum technologies.
Dr. Carmen Palacios-Berraquero, Founder and CEO of Nu Quantum said, “As quantum computing moves towards large-scale utility, collaboration becomes critical. The QDA brings the industry together to tackle the shared challenges of building quantum computing as infrastructure — scalable, interoperable, reliable and efficient — and ultimately making quantum compute accessible to the world, responsibly.”
Dame Wendy Hall, speaking about lessons from classical computing and AI,said, “It’s all about communication. It is so important to get the positive messages out about any new technology ahead of the inevitable scare stories about the risks and potential harms which the media love to pick up on. Of all the new technologies on the horizon though. Quantum computing is the hardest to explain to non technical audiences. That messaging will need a lot of work as the technology begins to emerge into the public arena.”
Hannah Boardman, Director responsible for AI, Quantum, Engineering Biology, Semiconductors, Robotics, Department for Science, Innovation & Technology , said, “Initiatives like this QDA show the power of bringing together different sections of the ecosystem across technologies, thinking in a different kind of way and focusing on delivering common goals to be identified in the room.”
Petrina Anne Steele, Head of Emerging Technologies at Equinix , said, “Quantum is an incubating technology that sits alongside classical HPC and now AI environments, and is highly complementary. Hybrid infrastructure is making quantum commercially actionable today. We already have companies doing high precision molecular modelling and exploring FX trading optimisation.”
Ben Bloom, Founder and CEO at Atom Computing , said, “Over the past two days, Nu Quantum and its partners have been exploring how to integrate quantum systems into a data center. This is an incredibly important topic as we continue to expand the reach of quantum computers to more and more industries and more and more users. Building a utility scale quantum computer doesn’t just fall to one company, and doesn’t even just fall to one technology. It’s the combination of multiple components together that will actually bring out a utility scale quantum computer.”
Looking ahead, the QDA will continue to convene industry leaders through future forums, working groups, and events, driving the industry toward scalable, robust, commercially viable quantum computing.
Photos can be found from the event here .
Get the latest research, company news, and market intelligence every week.
NVIDIA Corporation is an American multinational technology company and a global player in accelerated computing and Artificial Intelligence (AI). Founded in 1993, the company pushes the aerospace frontier with the Space-1 Vera Rubin Module, a platform for orbital data centers that delivers massive AI-compute Space Computing. This NVIDIA technology enables satellites and autonomous spacecraft to process and fuse sensor data rapidly Space Computing.
IBM is an iconic technology pioneer founded in 1911 as the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company and officially renamed International Business Machines Corporation in 1924. Beyond foundational computing, IBM possesses a deep legacy in aerospace and defense from building the guidance computers and Instrument Unit for NASA's historic Apollo missions to partnering with Airbus on CIMON, the first AI assistant on the ISS.
II-VI Incorporated, now known as Coherent Corp., is a leading global company specializing in the production of lasers and laser-based solutions. Their extensive product range serves various industrial, commercial, and scientific applications, making their technology integral to numerous sectors and industries.
Equinix specializes in digital infrastructure, operating a global network of data centers that provide colocation, connectivity, and managed solutions for enterprises, cloud providers, and network service providers. The company enables direct, secure interconnection between partners and platforms, supporting mission-critical applications, AI workloads, and hybrid multicloud environments. Equinix emphasizes reliability, scalability, and compliance, serving over 10,000 customers worldwide and facilitating digital transformation through its extensive ecosystem and advanced infrastructure.
Quantinuum is a quantum computing company advancing the aerospace sector through the development of algorithms for aerodynamic modeling, composite materials optimization, and sustainable aviation fuel cell engineering. Founded in 2021 through the merger of Cambridge Quantum and Honeywell Quantum Solutions, the firm provides high fidelity trapped ion hardware and software to accelerate industrial applications.
Atom Computing builds quantum computers using nuclear spin qubits formed from arrays of optically-trapped neutral atoms.
The Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) is a department of the government of the United Kingdom. Established in February 2023, DSIT took on policy responsibilities from the former Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy (BEIS) and the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport. The new department is responsible for helping to encourage, develop and manage the UK's scientific, research, and technological outputs. DSIT is also responsible for managing the necessary physical and digital infrastructure and regulation to support the British economy, UK public services, national security, and wider UK Government priorities.

The DSIT has launched a National Quantum Strategy, which is a 10-year vision and actions for the UK to be a leading quantum-enabled economy, recognizing the importance of quantum technologies for the UK's prosperity and security.
Nu Quantum develops Entanglement Fabric and Quantum Networking Units to interconnect discrete processing cores. Founded in 2018 as a Cambridge University spinout, the company's hardware enables secure quantum networks suitable for aerospace, aviation, and satellite telecommunications, facilitating distributed quantum computing.

articles.title_orig: USA Cycling Announces the 2026 UCI Para Cycling Track World Championships Team
articles.title_zh: USA Cycling Announces the 2026 UCI Para Cycling Track World Championships Team
articles.content_orig:
15 riders are set to compete in Apeldoorn, Netherlands on October 29-November 1, 2026.
The 2026 UCI Para-Cycling Track World Championships will take place October 29-November 1 in Apeldoorn, Netherlands, bringing the world’s best para cycling track athletes together for four days of racing.
Para Cycling track athletes compete across two divisions: Cycle (C), for riders on conventional bicycles with adaptations as needed, and Tandem (B), where visually impaired athletes race alongside a sighted pilot.
USA Cycling will field four tandems in Apeldoorn, including several returning athletes and new pairings.
Branden Walton (Livermore, Calif.) and pilot Ian Anderson (Fort Collins, Colo.) return to the World Championship boards after earning bronze in the Tandem Pursuit at last year’s World Championships in their first international event together. Michael Murphy and pilot Harrison Devine will make their World Championship debut as a tandem after impressing at this year’s National Championships, while Michael Stephens (Colorado Springs, Colo.) and pilot Joe Christiansen (Lyons, Colo.) will take on the sprint events. Current Pan-Am Champion Hannah Chadwick (Arcata, Calif.) will also race the tandem sprint events alongside her new pilot, Hayley Bates (Long Beach, Calif.).
In the C classes, Allison Jones (Colorado Springs, Colo.), Shawn Morelli (Meadville, Penn.), and Katie Walker (Chula Vista, Calif.) will all return to the World Championship boards. Morelli enters the competition as the reigning bronze medalist in the WC4 Scratch Race, and Jones is coming off her bronze medal in the 2026 UCI Para-Cycling Road World Championships Time Trial.
On the men’s side, four MC4 riders will represent the U.S., including Ryan Jastrab (Apple Valley, Calif.), Jason Macom ( Colorado Springs, Colo.), John Terrell (Colorado Springs, Colo.), and Brady Hout (Ronan, Mont.), who will make his World Championship debut.
“We’re really excited to take this team to Apeldoorn for the World Championships,” said Chris Furber, Senior Director of Para Cycling. “Last year we came away with two medals, and our ambition is to build on that performance. For us, it’s about adding value to performance, with every member of the team focused on how they can make a positive contribution to each athlete’s performance. Just as importantly, this is a learning environment. With only three major track events from here until the LA 2028 Games, we have limited opportunities to prepare our athletes at this level. We need to learn and improve quickly to make every opportunity count.”
USA Cycling will be supported in Apeldoorn by coaches Ben Sharp, a longtime Olympic and Paralympic medalist coach, and Pete Mitchell, a seven-time World Champion tandem pilot for Team GB.
The Team USA Roster is as follows:

articles.title_orig: U.S. officials seeking details of reported Russian plague death, quarantines
articles.title_zh: U.S. officials seeking details of reported Russian plague death, quarantines
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of people were reported to be in isolation after a Russian laboratory worker at an institute dedicated to studying the plague and other infectious diseases died of an undisclosed illness.
The researcher, a 28-year-old female laboratory technician at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia, in the town of Shelekhov, died after being diagnosed with a pneumonia of “unknown” origin, according to Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian agency that handles infectious disease.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that the administration was watching the situation closely .
“I don’t think it’s cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause to just keep an eye on it,” Rubio said.
Rospotrebnadzor has played down the link between the death of the researcher - named in local media as Darya Shipilova - and her work.
“No micro-organisms associated with the employee’s professional duties were detected in samples taken from the patient,” it asserted, adding that the “epidemiological situation” in the region was stable.
Nevertheless, the agency’s head, Anna Popova, traveled to Irkutsk on Friday, according to the local governor, Igor Kobzev, for what he described as an extraordinary meeting of the regional anti-epidemic commission.
The meeting was in connection with a “suspected case of a particularly dangerous infection affecting a resident of the region”, Kobzev said on Telegram.
Reached by phone on Monday, the institute where the researcher worked told CNN it was not commenting on the incident .
Regional authorities are implementing a “comprehensive set of anti-epidemic measures,” according to Maxim Modin, the mayor of the Shelekhovsky district in eastern Russia, near the Mongolian border.
The inpatient facility at the hospital where the worker was treated has been placed under quarantine, and several departments have stopped discharging or admitting patients, Modin said. Other hospitals in the region have also been closed, according to local media reports.
The woman’s death was confirmed by officials last week.
Ekaterina, a resident of Shekelov, told CNN on Monday that there were no visible changes in the city, but locals were anxious. “My acquaintances are slightly panicking,” she said.
Another resident, who wished to remain anonymous, said he was “shocked” by the news.
Unofficial reports, including by the independent regional news outlet Liudi Baikala, have said that nearly 200 people are under observation.
There have been no cases of infectious diseases reported among institute staff over the past 10 days, and all of the employee’s recent contacts are being tested and examined, Modin said.
In its only comment on the incident, the Kremlin said people should only trust updates coming from the official agency.
“One should rely on official statements from Rospotrebnadzor rather than listening to various rumors and speculation,”  Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Monday.
The World Health Organization told CNN it was in contact with the Russian health authorities to “verify the event, its circumstances, the laboratory tests underway, and their results.”
“Based on unofficial information available, the public health risk to the general population appears to be low,” it said.
Despite such reassurances, several countries in the region have put in place safeguarding measures.
Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Health said that while the risk was “very low”, the situation was being monitored and “sanitary and quarantine controls were implemented at state border crossing points.”
Uzbekistan said it “increased the readiness” of relevant authorities to deal with highly infectious diseases. Kyrgyzstan, which does not share a land border with Russia is some 1,500 miles from Irkutsk, announced Monday it was introducing quarantine controls at state border crossing points.
A virologist in Siberia, Alexander Chepurnov, told CNN that the strict protocols being followed were designed to prevent onward spread.
“After any suspected exposure, staff are instructed to immediately report it, decontaminate, undergo medical assessment and be isolated in a separate dedicated facility for however long they might be infectious,” Chepirnov said.
Angela Rassmussen, a virologist at the Vaccine and Infectious Disease Organization, told CNN that while pneumonic plague is deadly, it is not very transmissible and one would have to be exposed to a high bacterial load to become sick.
In that sense, it is unlike respiratory illnesses such as COVID, she said.
There is endemic plague among wildlife in parts of Siberia, Rassmussen added.
According to its website, the Anti-Plague Institute employs around 95 researchers and is a major public health facility responsible for monitoring and preventing outbreaks of high-risk bacterial and viral infections across Siberia and Russia’s Far East.
The head of the neighboring republic of Buryatia, Alexei Tsydenov, said earlier that the employee died “possibly from the plague,” but noted there had been no outbreak of the disease in his region.
Pneumonic plague is one of three types of plagues that are caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis.
The other two types typically spread from contact with infected fleas, animals or infected tissues.
An aluminum plant near the laboratory instructed staff to wear masks as a precautionary measure. The director of Irkutsk Aluminum Plant, Artem Fominikh, noted “conflicting reports” were circulating and called for calm.
Oldest known evidence of plague reveals the disease’s deadly impact 5,500 years ago
The infection in the Irkutsk region is “most likely not the plague, but even if confirmed, there will be no spread of this disease,” a former head of Rospotrebnadzor, Gennady Onishchenko, said on Friday.
Onishchenko told state news agency TASS that the onset of cold weather would likely prevent transmission.
A US State Department spokesperson told CNN Sunday that it was aware of the possible death due to pneumonic plague in Russia.
“We are monitoring the situation closely with the CDC and our other interagency partners,” the spokesperson said. “Many details have not been confirmed. We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly.”
Patients with pneumonic plague develop fever, headache, weakness and and “a rapidly developing pneumonia with shortness of breath, chest pain, cough, and sometimes bloody or watery mucous,” according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
The World Health Organization notes that the plague has a high fatality rate, but is also easily treated with antibiotics if caught early.
CNN’s Arina Porkhovnik, Logan Schiciano and Jamie Gumbrecht contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: What if the world hadn't built wind and solar?
articles.title_zh: What if the world hadn't built wind and solar?
articles.content_orig:
Twenty years ago, wind, solar and other non-hydro renewables were close to a rounding error. In 2005 they supplied a mere 2.0% of the world’s electricity generation. By 2015 that had risen to 6.8%, and by 2025 it was up to 19.8%. According to the IEA Electricity 2026 outlook, non-hydro renewables will supply around 21.8% of global electricity in 2026, edging past natural gas (21.6%) to become the second-largest source of power after coal. 1
That is a remarkable pace of growth from an industry that barely existed two decades ago. But not everyone is impressed; many commenters on social media have responded to these figures by pointing out that despite the growth of renewables, fossil fuel generation continues to grow as well. They aren’t wrong; global coal generation set a record in 2024. Gas generation reached a new high in 2025.
Their point is that clean energy isn’t replacing fossil fuels at all. It’s simply being piled on top of them to feed an ever-growing appetite for electricity, making this an “energy addition” rather than an energy transition. Global fossil electricity generation around 50% higher today than it was in 2005. Coal generation rose by 3,300 TWh and gas by 3,200 TWh. The world burns more coal for power now than it did when wind and solar started taking off.
This argument has been made in the past both by skeptics of growth and by energy systems modelers. The historian Jean-Baptiste Fressoz argues in More and More and More (2024) that “far from the industrial era passing through a series of transformations, each new phase has in practice remained almost wholly entangled with the previous one.” Coal mining created a huge new demand for timber for pit props, while the oil age ran on steel made with coal. Vaclav Smil has made the same point about today’s clean energy boom more bluntly: ”We use more fossil fuels today than at any time in history… Renewables are not replacing fossil fuels; are joining them.”
The problem with the “addition” argument is that it compares the world today with the world in 2005, rather than with the world as it would have been without clean energy. Electricity demand has not grown because wind turbines and solar panels were built. It has grown because of what the IEA describes as “rising consumption from industry, electric vehicles, air conditioning and data centers”. Demand growth is located overwhelmingly in emerging and developing economies, which accounted for about 80% of global demand growth in 2025 and an average of 95% over the past decade.
Global electricity demand rose by 75% (13,600 TWh) between 2005 and 2025. That demand had to be met by something. Wind and solar supplied 5,400 TWh of new demand, hydro 1,500 TWh, bioenergy and other renewables 530 TWh, nuclear 85 TWh, and fossil fuels the remaining 6,100 TWh. But over the past decade the balance has shifted sharply toward clean energy. Since 2015, wind and solar supplied 57% of demand growth, compared with 29% for fossil fuels. And in 2025, according to Ember’s Global Electricity Review 2026 , “wind and solar grew by 841 TWh, meeting 99% of global electricity demand growth”.
A 2024 study by Brantley Liddle found that “intermittent renewables (solar and wind) have unitary displacement effect.” In other words, each unit of wind and solar power displaced about one unit of coal and oil generation. Fossil generation has kept rising in many years because demand has grown faster than clean energy could be added. That is very different from clean energy failing to displace anything.
And electricity demand will continue to rapidly grow, particularly if we succeed in reducing global emissions by electrifying sectors of the economy that currently burn fossil fuels. Most scenarios where we reach net zero emissions involve a doubling or tripling of electricity generation.
So if we want to assess the real world emissions impact of wind and solar buildout over the past 20 years, the right question to ask is not “did fossil use go down?” but rather “how much higher would it have been?”
To answer this, I built a counterfactual for the global power sector in which wind and solar (and geothermal, which is less than 2% of the total) stopped growing in 2005. In every separate country, their generation is held at 2005 levels, while electricity demand, nuclear, hydro and bioenergy follow their real-world paths. 2 The missing clean generation has to come from somewhere, and in this counterfactual it comes from fossil fuels.
The key choice is which fossil fuels are used to fill in the gap. A wind farm in China or India displaces coal, while one in Texas or the UK mostly displaces gas. So rather than assuming a single global fossil mix, the analysis fills each country’s gap with that country’s own coal, gas and oil mix in each year, using data for about 200 countries from Ember . This keeps real-world coal-to-gas switching like what occurred during the US shale gas boom in place, rather than crediting it to renewables. 3
Without wind and solar growth since 2005, global power-sector CO2 emissions in 2025 would have been 28% higher, at 16.9 billion tonnes rather than 13.2 billion. This adds up to 3.7 billion tonnes avoided in 2025, which is about three-quarters of the total CO2 US emissions that year (or roughly 1.5x EU emissions).
Between 2006 and 2025, wind and solar avoided about 23 billion tonnes of CO2. The biggest assumption I’ve made is what fossil fuel fills in the gap: if every missing kilowatt-hour had come from gas, avoided emissions would be 15 billion tonnes, while if it was all coal it would have been 30 billion.
This lines up almost exactly with Ember’s own estimate. Using a simpler method (and a 2000 baseline rather than 2005 baseline), Ember’s Global Electricity Review 2026 found that “had wind and solar not grown since 2000, fossil generation would have been 30% higher in 2025, and emissions 28% higher.”
While its true that global electricity emissions have yet to clearly peak, it may well be imminent; emissions went down in 2025 and may be on track to decline in 2026 as well, though rapid increases in demand from vehicle electrification and data centers have made this a bit more challenging. 4 But there are many countries in which electricity emissions have already peaked and declined substantially, and where clean energy has played a key role in those declines.
Globally, clean energy has not yet led to fossil fuel use peaking in the electricity sector. In 2025, fossil generation was essentially flat (down ~0.3%). But that global total hides a lot of country-level variability. In many wealthier economies, where demand has grown more slowly, clean energy has driven real emissions reductions (even when accounting for the outsourcing of some industrial production).
Between 2005 and 2025, power-sector CO2 emissions fell by 75% in the UK, 55% in the European Union and 37% in the United States.
The reasons why differ from place to place:
In the EU, wind and solar account for about 85% of the decline (512 of 601 million tonnes), even though falling nuclear output pushed emissions up by about 100 million tonnes.
In the UK, the decline had three main drivers: wind and solar (56 million tonnes), lower domestic generation (58 million tonnes, partly because the UK now imports more power), and the near-elimination of coal, which went from 45% of UK fossil generation to effectively zero (36 million tonnes).
In the US, switching from coal to cheaper natural gas cut emissions by 682 million tonnes, slightly more than wind and solar (606 million tonnes), while a 12% rise in electricity use added 352 million tonnes. Coal’s share of US fossil generation fell from 69% to 29%.
Without wind and solar growth, EU power emissions would have fallen by only about 16% since 2005 rather than 55%, US emissions by about 17% rather than 37%, and UK emissions by about 53% rather than 75%. In these regions clean energy has not just met new demand, its actually pushed fossil generation d

articles.title_orig: Jay Wheeler Announces ‘La Voz Favorita’ World Tour, Kicking Off Late 2026
articles.title_zh: Jay Wheeler Announces ‘La Voz Favorita’ World Tour, Kicking Off Late 2026
articles.content_orig:
Get Pollstar News and more delivered right to your inbox with Pollstar Daily Pulse.
By signing up, you agree to Pollstar’s Privacy Policy and Terms of Use
Puerto Rican artist Jay Wheeler has announced the “La Voz Favorita” World Tour, produced by Dynamic Records in partnership with AUL Worldwide and UTA, taking the urban music star to major venues across Europe, the United States and Latin America beginning December 2026.
Presale begins Wednesday, Oct. 7 at 11:00 a.m. local time, while the general onsale starts Friday, October 9 at 11:00 a.m. local time.
“La Voz Favorita” Tour 2026 will kick off in Spain on December 4, 2026, in Tenerife, followed by stops in Gran Canaria, Málaga, Valencia, Bilbao, Madrid and Barcelona, where the European leg will conclude on Dec. 19 with a performance at Palau Sant Jordi.
In March 2027, Wheeler will bring the tour to the United States, with performances in major markets and venues including MGM Music Hall in Boston, Kaseya Center in Miami, Coca Cola Roxy in Atlanta, Fillmore in Denver, YouTube Theater in Los Angeles and many others, with Latin America dates in April and June at markets including Quito, Lima, Tegucigalpa, Guatemala City, Mexico City, Buenos Aires, Santiago, Panama City, San José, Bogotá and Santo Domingo.
“This La Voz Favorita tour is going to be very special. Seeing and hearing all my fans sing along to my songs is one of the most beautiful parts of this career, and I feel truly blessed to have the opportunity to experience it all over again,” said Jay Wheeler.
The tour marks a new chapter in Wheeler’s career, according to the announcement, with Wheeler’s new album seeing multiple hits including “De Lejitos,” which reached No. 1 on Billboard Latin Airplay and Latin Rhythm Airplay, while also reaching No. 7 on Billboard Hot Latin Songs, where it remained in the Top 10 for 11 consecutive weeks.
The booking agency for the tour is AUL Worldwide, with offices in Miami, Los Angeles, Bogotá and Mexico City, led by founder and CEO Adrian Urgelles, who has overseen Jay’s touring alongside with Dynamic Records since 2023.

articles.title_orig: U.S. B-1 bombers evacuated from UK base after attack threats from Iran
articles.title_zh: U.S. B-1 bombers evacuated from UK base after attack threats from Iran
articles.content_orig:
The United States moved all of its long-range bombers stationed in the United Kingdom back to their American home bases on Sunday after an unspecified new threat, according to a US official. It comes days after the British government arrested a number of individuals in connection with an alleged Iranian plot to target the UK airbase where the planes had been stationed.
“We can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” the official told CNN. The statement did not include details on why the planes were moved.
The source familiar called the latest threat a “real world incident.” It is unusual that the US military would move the bombers back to their home stations instead of deploying them to another base in the region, the official said.
Vice President JD Vance said Monday that the move was made “out of an abundance of caution,” suggesting it was a response to a potential threat from Iran even as he declined to detail the specific concerns.
“I think that we’re going to be as careful as we possibly can be,” Vance told reporters. “We do feel with some confidence that the Iranians are, you know, they’re trying to do what the Iranian state has done for 49 years, which is engage in acts of terrorism against the United States and against a lot of other people as well.”
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, downplayed the removal of the US bombers, saying he would not “directly tie” the planes’ redeployment to the alleged Iranian plot.
“The only reason why you guys are focused on how many planes are at Fairford is because of the threat that happened last week. But it’s not unusual to see rotations happen and movement of assets to different parts of the world based on exercises, redeployments, people changing out and new people coming in, new planes coming in, old planes going out,” Rubio told reporters at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on Monday.
Rubio added that the United States had worked closely on security with the UK for a long time, including on the Fairford investigation.
A Downing Street spokesperson said that the UK government would not comment on foreign nations’ military operations. Asked about safety concerns by residents living near the base, the spokesperson told reporters that the UK has “the tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country, but not just that, throughout the world.”
The UK Ministry of Defense also declined to comment on the operations or capabilities of other nations.
The Royal Air Force base at Fairford has been used to deploy US B-1 bombers involved in the war against Iran and is an operating location for US Global Strike Command, which is tasked with managing long-distance strikes.
CNN national security analyst Alex Plitsas said it was likely several dozen bombers were stationed at Fairford, adding that it was unusual to move all the aircraft.
“It speaks to the credibility and the seriousness of the threat overall to the base that we’re talking about,” he told Ben Hunte on CNN Newsroom.
The relocation of the bombers comes amid the investigation into the alleged plot. British police on September 27 arrested five men on suspicion of terror and explosives offenses close to the airbase.
The men – identified only as British nationals between the ages of 23 and 25 and from the London area – were quickly released on bail, with police confirming no explosives were found in three vans at the scene. Their release sparked criticism from President Donald Trump, who said “I wouldn’t have done that.”
A 25-year-old British-Iranian dual national was also arrested on Thursday in connection with the alleged plot.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last week there are “strong indications” Iran was involved in the incident.
“We will say more in due course, but we can confirm our belief that we believe Iran to have played a part,” he told the BBC on Sept 30.
Burnham’s remarks appeared to support the US’ assessment that the incident involved a foreign actor. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said “the hands of a foreign actor” were involved in the alleged plot but declined to provide details in an interview with Fox News last week.
“I think it ties us to the reality here. We are dealing with elements in the world, and in the case of Iran for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally,” he said.
Meanwhile, Iran has denied any involvement in the incident, described the accusations as baseless and summoned the British ambassador in Tehran, Iranian state media reported Thursday. During the meeting, Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Majid Takht-Ravanchi reportedly urged London to revise what he called its “inappropriate approach” toward Tehran.
This has been updated with additional details.
CNN’s Nic Robertson, Max Saltman, Chandler Thornton Tim Lister and James Frater contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: XP Inc. and Other Stocks Surging After Brazil’s Election Shock
articles.title_zh: XP Inc. and Other Stocks Surging After Brazil’s Election Shock
articles.content_orig:
Brazil is heading for another Lula-Bolsonaro showdown. But this time it is Jair Bolsonaro’s eldest son Flávio who stands between leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and another term in power.
A Bolsonaro victory would push the region further towards the right, hand US President Donald Trump a powerful ideological ally in its largest country and potentially strengthen Washington’s hand as it seeks to counter China’s influence across the hemisphere.
For Lula, 80, the runoff vote leaves one of Latin America’s most prominent left-wing leaders fighting for what is likely will be last term if he wins.
Together, Lula and Bolsonaro accounted for more than 92% of the votes, underscoring the strong grip of the Lula and Bolsonaro camps on Brazilian politics.
But neither secured the 50% needed to avoid a runoff, now set for October 25.
The situation now resembles that of 2022, but Bolsonaro performed better than his father did in the first round four years ago.
The crucial battleground was the Southeast, where nearly 40% of the electorate lives. There, Flávio won São Paulo and Minas Gerais.
His victory in Minas Gerais carries particular symbolic weight: the state has voted for the winner in every presidential election since 1989 when Brazil held its first direct presidential election after military rule.
The result suggests Bolsonaro, who exceeded poll projections, has done more than simply inherit his father’s political movement. He may have expanded it.
With a campaign focused on crime and the economy, he secured nearly four percentage points more than his father in the first round in 2022. He leaned heavily on his father’s image while also seeking to present himself as a more moderate figure.
For Lula, the result raises an uncomfortable question. Can his political legacy and record in office still deliver an electoral majority?
Minas Gerais helps explain his predicament. He received 43.21% there, well below the 48.3% won in the first round of 2022. Nor did he achieve the lead margin his campaign had hoped for in the Northeast, his main stronghold.
The runoff will depend on who can capture voters who backed eliminated candidates and whether either side can mobilize Brazilians who stayed home on Sunday.
The eliminated candidates collectively accounted for 7.82% of votes.
Most of those votes went to candidates on the center-right or right, potentially giving Bolsonaro another advantage.
But abstention is another potentially decisive reservoir of votes. About 21% of eligible voters did not cast a ballot, and mobilizing them could tip the scales in a tight election.
Polls leading up to Sunday showed the two candidates tied in runoff scenarios.
Lula must now overcome a first-round deficit amid voter concerns over purchasing power and crime, an issue Bolsonaro made central to his campaign, as well as controversies surrounding key figures in scandals seen as close to the president.
Bolsonaro, meanwhile, enters the runoff with another advantage: political momentum beyond the presidential race. His party and allies won numerous Senate seats as well as governorships in key states, potentially giving a Bolsonaro presidency significant legislative and regional support.
An even more polarized runoff is expected. Lula will likely frame the vote as a referendum on democracy and while Bolsonaro will focus on his tough-on-crime rhetoric and allegations of corruption against Lula and his party.
Few outside Brazil have more riding on the runoff than Trump. The US president openly endorsed Bolsonaro earlier in the campaign and maintains a tense relationship with Lula’s government.
He has been notably quieter in recent weeks but there is little ambiguity over which outcome would better suit Washington.
Since Trump returned to the White House, no left-wing candidate has won a presidential election in Latin America. Now, Washington hopes to bring about an ideological shift in Brazil, the region’s biggest economy , that will help it fully impose its “Donroe Doctrine” and contain China’s influence.
“Trump had already welcomed Bolsonaro to the Oval Office at the White House and has imposed punitive tariffs on Brazil, the sole motivation for which appears to be political,” international relations expert Farid Kahhat, a professor at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, told CNN.
“The fact that he hasn’t spoken out publicly again doesn’t change the fact that he already did so in the past and that he has made public policy decisions in favor of the Bolsonaros,” he added.
For Kahhat, Trump’s recent restraint may itself be strategic.
“They’ve already decided it was better to keep a lower profile,” he said.
There is good reason for caution. Open intervention by Trump could have the opposite effect in the world’s tenth-largest economy, which is far less dependent on Washington than some of its neighbors.
“They’ve noticed that in Brazil, [interference] might not work the same way as it does in Honduras or Colombia,” Kahhat said.
Lula has also used the banner of national sovereignty as a campaign weapon.
Political scientist Manuel Alcántara Sáez, director of the International Center for Political and Social Studies (CIEPS-AIP) in Panama, said another Trump intervention could end up helping Lula.
“It would be more beneficial for Lula because there is a stronger sentiment against US interference,” he said.
Trump isn’t the only regional ally to have backed Bolsonaro. Argentine President Javier Milei supported him and attended his campaign launch, where he hurled insults at Lula.
“Since then, I haven’t noticed Milei getting so involved in the campaign,” Alexander Main, director of international policy at the Center for Economic and Policy Research, told CNN. “I think maybe they felt it wasn’t helping that much.”
But Bolsonaro’s strong showing quickly drew celebration from the Latin American right. Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella who won in June with Trump’s backing said on X: “May God have mercy on our brother country as He did on Colombia. True change is defeating the left.”
Milei followed by congratulating Bolsonaro, saying: “The American continent is made up of citizens who want to live in freedom.”
Bolsonaro’s performance appears, at first glance, to fit neatly into Latin America’s broader rightward turn. But analysts caution that something more complicated may be happening.
With strategies based on antagonism and the “cancellation” of the opponent, policy proposals and promises “matter very little” in convincing undecided voters, Alcántara Sáez said.
Beyond the committed bases, “the rest of the electorate is driven by other kinds of impulses, including fatigue and despair at seeing, on one side, an 80-year-old candidate and, on the other, a candidate who is the son of someone in prison, convicted of leading an attempted coup,” he said.
That fatigue echoes a broader pattern across Latin America: incumbent parties struggling to survive voter frustration.
Kahhat said that although “this is a time of crisis for the left throughout the region,” the string of right-wing victories should not necessarily be read as a wholesale ideological conversion.
“It depends on the context, but it is not necessarily a rejection of left-wing movements as such, but rather of those in power at a time of great economic instability,” he said.
Brazil’s runoff will therefore test two competing explanations for the political transformation sweeping the region: whether Latin America is undergoing a durable shift to the right, or whether frustrated voters are simply punishing whoever happens to be in power.
For Alcántara Sáez, there is another dividing line that may prove just as important: how Latin American governments position themselves toward Trump.

articles.title_orig: University of Lynchburg ranked by U.S. News & World Report, The Princeton Review
articles.title_zh: University of Lynchburg ranked by U.S. News & World Report, The Princeton Review
articles.content_orig:
U.S. News & World Report and The Princeton Review have ranked the University of Lynchburg among the nation’s best colleges and universities.
In its 2027 edition of “Best Colleges,” U.S. News ranked Lynchburg 332nd among National Universities and 154th in the Top Private Schools category. Lynchburg’s nursing program ranked 557th, and the University ranked 329th in Top Performers on Social Mobility, which recognizes schools that “performed best in … Pell Grant graduation rates and Pell Grant graduation rate performance.”
Lynchburg also is listed in “The Best 392 Colleges: 2027 Edition,” published by The Princeton Review. Lynchburg also was ranked among The Princeton Review’s “Best Mid-Atlantic” colleges and universities.
“These recognitions demonstrate the strength of the University of Lynchburg community,” said Dr. Sally Selden, the University’s president. “We offer an education grounded in academic excellence, personal connection, and student engagement.
“Our students thrive because they are supported by faculty and staff who are deeply committed to their success, both in and out of the classroom. I’m proud of the work happening across our campus and grateful that our student experience is being recognized nationally.”
According to U.S. News, its “Best Colleges” are “ranked according to their performance across widely accepted indicators of excellence.” You can read more about the methodology U.S. News uses to compile its rankings here .
The Princeton Review stated that its 2027 list “brings together survey results from over 172,000 students across the country to find out what they love the most about these schools in everything from financial aid and career services to sustainability and quality of life.”
Those surveyed about the University of Lynchburg described its students as “friendly and willing to work together and help each other out” and said the University was “beginning to have more cultural diversity.” Its reputation for “Southern hospitality” was also noted.
One student put it this way: “Everyone is very helping. If someone is not able to help you with a homework question or a project, then they will find you someone who can. It does feel like one giant family here.”
You can read more about The Princeton Review’s methodology here .

articles.title_orig: Teenager's hand blown off during confrontation between France school protesters and police
articles.title_zh: Teenager's hand blown off during confrontation between France school protesters and police
articles.content_orig:
A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators near a school in France, an official has said, as student protests continue across the country.
The "very serious incident" happened in the northern city of Lens on Monday morning, according to the prefect of Pas-de-Calais, François-Xavier Lauch.
"The student's life is not in danger," he said, adding that the teenager was transferred "very quickly" to a hospital nearby.
Around 500 schools were partially or totally closed across the country on Monday amid student protests over the condition of school buildings and staffing which have led to clashes with police in recent days.
There are mixed reports in French media about how the boy came to sustain the injury.
AFP news agency, citing a police union source, reported that the student appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which exploded in his hand.
However, regional newspaper La Voix Du Nord quoted a girl, who was reportedly standing near the teenager, as saying he did not pick up the grenade.
"He didn't pick it up. I was there, I saw it. He didn't pick it up, he didn't catch it," she was quoted as saying.
When asked about the incident, Lens Mayor Sylvain Robert said the circumstances still needed to be clarified.
"Like you, and like many others, I have seen some videos showing the aftermath. But I did not see how the operation was organised, either by the police or by the students," he told French media.
A regional prosecutor said an investigation would be carried out by the French police watchdog, the General Inspection of the National Police (IGPN), "so all light can be shed on what happened".
The incident took place close to the Auguste Béhal high school, the prefect said.
Lauch said a "larger gathering" of students than on previous days had assembled outside the school.
"At the start of the morning, they threw various projectiles at the local police officers who were on site initially. When I say projectiles, I mean stones, fireworks, and mortars," he told French media.
"Instructions were given by the interdepartmental director of the National Police, naturally with my approval, to deploy a company of riot police (CRS) here to maintain order, and it was in this context that this event occurred."
The school issued a statement on Monday morning, saying: "In light of the events that took place this morning and in order to ensure the safety of the entire school community, the institution is switching to distance learning from now on.
"In addition, to support everyone during this period, a listening and support unit has also been set up at the establishment."
According to education minister Édouard Geffray, at least 190 students have been injured since the protests began.
Last week, Eden, 14, was badly hurt in Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône after reportedly being struck in the head by a tear gas grenade.
The student suffered "a double jaw fracture" and had to undergo "extremely major surgery", according to his lawyer. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has announced an investigation.
Speaking at a news conference on Monday, Eden's mother said her heart was "shattered".
"His jaw is wired shut. He can't eat except through a straw and only liquids," French media outlet BFMTV reported her as saying.
"It's shameful, it's appalling, it's violent, it's horrific," she said, adding: "This should not happen. They are dealing with children who are asking for better conditions in which to study."
The recent wave of protests began in late September in Paris and has spread across the country.
High school students started the demonstrations, complaining about a lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings. University students joined last week, making similar demands.
More than 5,000 people have been arrested altogether since the start of the movement, according AFP, with around 85% of them minors.
The radical left La France Insoumise (LFI) party leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon described the protests as the "most powerful high school and university student youth movement" since 1968 - a major year of French protest, which saw millions of workers go on strike.
Education minister Geffray said Monday saw a "clear decrease" in the number of schools disrupted compared to recent days, with 589 institutions affected.
Last Friday, French authorities said 735 of France's 3,700 schools had been disrupted.
But France is braced for more large protests on Tuesday, as student organisation Union Syndicale Lycéenne (USL) has again called on people to take to the streets.
Other organisations, including the teachers' union SNES-FSU, have also shown their support for the students, urging their members to join tomorrow's protest.
In response, the French government said it would set up a "major consultation platform" for students from across the country to share details of the difficulties they have experienced.
Geffray said he hoped to resolve "most of the problematic situations" by 16 October.

articles.title_orig: United Methodist elected federation world vice president
articles.title_zh: United Methodist elected federation world vice president
articles.content_orig:
Patricia Petudzai Mapani, 61, a United Methodist from Harare, was elected world vice president of the World Federation of Methodist and Uniting Church Women on Aug. 27 at the organization’s world assembly in Auckland, New Zealand.
The Chisipiti United Methodist Church member has held several leadership positions in the organization over the past two decades.
She served as president of the South and East Africa Area 2022-2026 and vice president of the area 2016-2022. Before that, Mapani was The United Methodist Church in Zimbabwe’s unit coordinator for eight years.
“I am driven by passion to support, encourage, empower women and girls and being the voice of the voiceless,” she told UM News.
“It was a very tight election and I felt most humbled to have been chosen. I am still in awe. I am very thankful to the Almighty God for the opportunity to serve at a global level,” Mapani said.
As area president she expanded the area from eight to 18 units, increased attendance at seminars and established the Africa University Scholarship Fund, which enables disadvantaged young women to pursue higher education. She also introduced monthly dawn prayer meetings that are held virtually and have strengthened spiritual life of members in the area.
Her vision is to faithfully strengthen the federation by supporting the world president, coordinating materials and United Nations programs, promoting prayer, women’s empowerment and sustainable partnerships, and safeguarding and sustaining Christ’s transforming mission through hope, unity and love.
Chikwanah is a UM News correspondent based in Harare, Zimbabwe.

articles.title_orig: World Food Program USA and Suzanne Collins Call on Hunger Games Fans to Help Deliver One Million Meals to Families Facing Hunger Around the World
articles.title_zh: World Food Program USA and Suzanne Collins Call on Hunger Games Fans to Help Deliver One Million Meals to Families Facing Hunger Around the World
articles.content_orig:
The global fan challenge celebrates the upcoming release of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping by Lionsgate, based on Suzanne Collins' bestselling novel, and offers multiple ways to help create a world without hunger
WASHINGTON , Oct. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Ahead of the theatrical release of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping on November 20, 2026 , World Food Program USA, Suzanne Collins, and Lionsgate today launched a global fan challenge to deliver one million meals to families facing hunger around the world. This challenge is part of a robust campaign to raise awareness and critical funds for global hunger during the end-of-year giving season. Fans can use their generosity, creativity, and voices to help build a hunger-free world by taking action at wfpusa.org/HungerGamesMovie .
"Freedom from hunger is a basic human right, which is why my family has long supported World Food Program USA," said Suzanne Collins. "Please join us in spreading the word about the need to secure adequate nutrition for our neighbors around the world."
Every fan action supports the mission of the World Food Programme (WFP), which delivers food and hope to families across the globe when they need it most. To get started, fans can visit wfpusa.org/HungerGamesMovie to learn more and take the following actions powered by the Zero Hunger Generation, World Food Program USA's youth movement for students and young professionals to help end world hunger.
Fans can do even more with the Zero Hunger Generation . For a limited time, Zero Hunger Generation members can join a Hunger Games book club and post a reaction to the film upon its release to earn special The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping badges and certificates. Through the Zero Hunger Generation program, World Food Program USA is mobilizing a community of young people around hunger relief with educational, service-oriented, and career-building activities.
Today, over 260 million people globally experience severe hunger. In the hardest-to-reach places on Earth, WFP is there saving lives in emergencies and using food assistance to build a pathway to peace, stability, and prosperity for people recovering from conflict, disasters, and the impact of extreme weather.
To reach fans across the globe, World Food Program USA will deploy a campaign alongside Lionsgate, WFP, and ShareTheMeal that cuts across social media, digital advertising, email, SMS, a U.S. TV public service announcement, and that will feature special messages from cast members calling on fans to get involved. World Food Program USA's goal is to help fans learn how small actions can make a big impact and inspire the next generation of hunger relief advocates.
"We are grateful to our generous partners Suzanne Collins and Charles Pryor, and Lionsgate, for helping us engage Hunger Games fans in the movement to end global hunger," said Barron Segar, President and CEO of World Food Program USA. "Hunger is one of the world's most urgent crises, but it is also solvable. By donating, sharing a message of hope, or lending their voice, this generation of fans can become part of the solution."
*Fans ages 18+ can donate at wfpusa.org/HungerGamesMovie.
About World Food Program USA:
World Food Program USA, a 501(c)(3) organization based in Washington, D.C., proudly supports the mission of the World Food Programme by mobilizing American policymakers, businesses and individuals to advance the global movement to end hunger. To learn more, visit wfpusa.org/mission-history .
About the World Food Programme:
The United Nations World Food Programme is the world's largest humanitarian organization saving lives in emergencies and using food assistance to build a pathway to peace, stability and prosperity for people recovering from conflict, disasters and the impact of climate change.
Lionsgate (NYSE: LION) is one of the world's leading standalone, pure play, publicly-traded content companies. It brings together diversified motion picture and television production and distribution businesses, a world-class portfolio of valuable brands and franchises, a premier talent management and production powerhouse at 3 Arts Entertainment and a more than 20,000-title film and television library, all driven by Lionsgate's bold and entrepreneurial culture.
Suzanne Collins is the internationally bestselling author of the Hunger Games series, which includes the novels The Hunger Games, Catching Fire, Mockingjay, The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, and Sunrise on the Reaping. Together, the books have sold over 100 million copies and were the basis for five popular films. Her other books include the acclaimed Underland Chronicles series, which begins with Gregor the Overlander, and the picture book Year of the Jungle, illustrated by James Proimos. To date, her books have been published in fifty-five languages around the world.

articles.title_orig: Chicago is the world’s most climate-resilient city. Loyola helped it get there
articles.title_zh: Chicago is the world’s most climate-resilient city. Loyola helped it get there
articles.content_orig:
Chicago topped the list of the world’s most climate-resilient cities, as evaluated by AlphaGeo, a Singapore-based company that ranked 72 of the world’s largest cities based on their exposure to climate risks and ability to reduce adverse impacts from extreme weather events.
“The good news is they call us out and highlight what we have here in Chicago, which is plentiful, clean water and relatively good air quality,” says Aaron Durnbaugh, director of sustainability at Loyola University Chicago. “Although we’re seeing more extreme weather in Chicago, it’s not what folks deal with on the coasts with hurricanes and typhoons or in heavily wooded landscapes prone to wildfires.”
Durnbaugh, a former deputy commissioner in the City of Chicago’s Department of the Environment and one of the chief architects of its pioneering 2008 Climate Action Plan , says Chicago’s privileged geographical location only tells part of the story. The city’s decades-long focus on climate adaptation planning has paid off in infrastructure upgrades, power grid diversification, and emergency response systems that have helped Chicago brace itself for the hostile effects of shifting climate patterns.
Two measures, in particular, stand out.
—
                                    Gilbert Michaud, assistant professor of environmental policy in the School of Environmental Sustainability
Following a heat wave in 1995 that led to the deaths of more than 700 Chicagoans, many of them older adults and people of color, the city invested in new cooling centers, launched wellness checks for at-risk residents, and fortified its power grid to prevent the kind of rolling brownouts that left tens of thousands of residents without power and air conditioning for days during the heat wave.
The city also bolstered its stormwater management infrastructure, widening piping conduits in its combined sewer system, leveraging plant-based infrastructure to absorb rainwater, and partnering with the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District of Greater Chicago to advance the development of the Deep Tunnel, a 110-mile-long infrastructure system begun in the 1970s and still underway that conveys water to reservoirs and treatment plants through massive underground tunnels.
“We’ve done a lot of things here in our region to improve our infrastructure, including our social infrastructure,” Durnbaugh said. “We’ve created cooling centers. We’ve created social service and public health programs that make sure that people are safe. At the same time, we’ve invested a lot in the hardening of our grid, so that electricity is available even under the most extreme or peak conditions.”
If the recognition comes as welcome news for the city, it is also an auspicious sign for Loyola, whose climate adaptation vision is guided by the Office of Sustainability and the School of Environmental Sustainability and closely aligned with Loyola’s Jesuit mission and commitment to integral ecology.
Under the leadership of Durnbaugh and others, Loyola’s 2015-2025 Climate Action Plan, A Just Future , positioned it to become the first university in the Chicago area to achieve carbon neutrality for its primary energy use. The University’s progress toward net-zero emissions has fulfilled several recent milestones, including a commitment to 100 percent renewable electricity ; $150 million invested in high-performing buildings and the long-term Campus Plan ; the growth of SES; and the inclusion of sustainability in the University’s core undergraduate curriculum.
“Both the city and Loyola have recent climate action plans,” says Gilbert Michaud, an assistant professor of environmental policy in the School of Environmental Sustainability. “What I really appreciate is that we’re actually taking tangible steps to achieve them. One of the things you see with these roadmaps is the real rubber hits the road, in terms of implementation. And that’s what gets me excited about Loyola. We’re walking the walk, we’re achieving our targets, and the city is too.”
Durnbaugh cites several efforts that have helped Loyola draw national attention for its climate resiliency efforts—and they go well beyond decarbonization. In the 1990s, when erosion threatened the stability of high-rises south of campus, Loyola built a sea wall along Lake Michigan to fortify the shoreline near Santa Clara Hall, and raised several building foundations to prevent groundwater infiltration.
More recently, Loyola expanded a chiller plant to keep buildings cool in the face of warming temperatures, created text-based emergency alert systems, and implemented an extensive stormwater management system that includes 17 green roofs spanning more than 55,000 square feet , along with rain gardens, semi-permeable walkways, and underground stormwater infiltration vaults. The system diverts an estimated 19 million gallons of water from city sewers annually—enough to connect Chicago to Houston with one-gallon water jugs.
“Our stormwater system is not just taking pressure off of someone down the sewershed from us,” Durnbaugh said. “But also because we’re next to Lake Michigan, we can direct that water where, historically, it used to go, which is back out to Lake Michigan.”
Perhaps the biggest recent energy transition the University has undergone is a 12-year power purchase agreement with Constellation that began on January 1, 2025. Through the fixed-position contract, Loyola has agreed to buy an estimated 81,660 megawatt hours of electricity annually from the Double Black Diamond solar farm, the largest utility-scale solar project east of the Mississippi River.
The solar energy agreement, aligned with Illinois’ target for zero emissions by 2050 under the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act , helps Loyola bring more clean, renewable energy onto the PJM regional transmission grid that feeds into ComEd’s local distribution network. Since electricity pricing fluctuates with demand, on hot summer days and cold winter days when electricity is in heavy use, Loyola can earn money back.
“We’re signing a contract to lock in the purchase of renewable energy at a fixed rate,” Michaud said. “Not only is it good from a climate and renewable energy standpoint, but it’s also a hedge against future fuel price increases.”
These efforts, along with students’ active role in biodiesel production, waste diversion, and urban agriculture programs, helped Loyola earn the Platinum rating —the highest possible—from the Association for the Advancement of Sustainability in Higher Education (AASHE) in their Sustainability Tracking, Assessment & Rating System (STARS). Loyola is the first institution in the Midwest to achieve the Platinum designation and joins only 10 other U.S.-based and seven international institutions in receiving the distinction.
Soon, Michaud says, that number could grow as other universities look to pioneering schools like Loyola as models.
“You have other colleges and campuses that are sort of looking at what we’re doing and having conversations with their faculty and staff, and maybe up to the president and board of trustees. Like, should we be doing this too? Should we also invest in solar? Should we also invest in high-performing buildings?”
Durnbaugh and Michaud are, of course, not the only climate resiliency experts at Loyola who have had a hand in shaping Chicago’s climate adaptation strategy.
Karen Weigert, the director of the Baumhart Center for Social Enterprise and Responsibility at the Quinlan School of Business, was the City of Chicago’s first chief sustainability officer, a position created under former mayor Rahm Emanuel. During her tenure, she led the development of the Sustainable Chicago Action Agenda that laid out 24 goals and more than 100 action items to help make the city more livable under changing climate conditions.
Though pleased by the city’s recent designation, she says there is plenty of work still to be done to prepare for growing climate hazards and extend resiliency efforts equitably across Chic

articles.title_orig: Inovonics Will Acquire Broadcast Tools Inc.
articles.title_zh: Inovonics Will Acquire Broadcast Tools Inc.
articles.content_orig:
Update your browser to view this website correctly. Update my browser now
Home › News and Business › Business and Law
Broadcast Tools Inc., a manufacturer of specialty and “problem-solving” products for broadcast, will be acquired by Inovonics Broadcast.
Founder and President Donald Winget informed his dealers in a letter on Thursday.
“After nearly 40 years in business, I am finally ready to retire,” he wrote.
BTI is based in Sedro Woolley, Wash. Winget wrote that Inovonics will continue the Broadcast Tools name and product line, moving production to its location in Felton, Calif.
“Ben Barber and his team at Inovonics are fully committed to maintaining the excellence of our products and to nurturing the relationships of trust that have been built with you, our dealers, over these many years.”
BTI products include analog and AES routers, remote controls, satellite channel controllers, analog mixers and DAs, silence monitors and program schedulers.
Winget began in broadcasting as a gofer for the chief engineer of a radio station in Eau Claire, Wis., according to a company history on its website. He served in the U.S. Army during the Vietnam war and later started an engineering contracting business, moving it to the Seattle area in the 1970s. Winget and engineer Lee Hurley created Sentry Systems, an early PC-based automation systems.
Winget founded BTI in 1989 while he was chief engineer at KXRX in Seattle. ( Read a company history .)
Inovonics was founded by Jim Wood and Mark Drake in 1972 to make drop-in, replacement tape recorder electronics assemblies for reel-to-reel machines. The company’s line today includes processors, monitors, RDS products, streaming gear and other specialty broadcast items.

articles.title_orig: Multiple Security Failures Allowed FlyDubai Pilot Into Cockpit
articles.title_zh: Multiple Security Failures Allowed FlyDubai Pilot Into Cockpit
articles.content_orig:
An Israeli airline El Al aircraft is parked on the tarmac at Ben Gurion Airport near the city of Lod on Friday. Jack Guez/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
TEL AVIV, Israel — An ongoing investigation into last week's midair attack on a FlyDubai plane has found that the co-pilot who tried to take control of the flight intended to crash it into Israel's Ben Gurion International Airport, a person familiar with the matter but not authorized to speak publicly told NPR.
The plane was flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv and was intending to land at Ben Gurion midmorning on a busy weekday. The co-pilot attacked the plane's captain midflight with an axe and attempted to take control of the plane.
It is believed that the co-pilot likely acted alone, the source said.
Authorities in the United Arab Emirates — which is leading the main investigation into the incident, with help from Israeli officials — and in Israel have deemed the attack an attempted terrorist attack, although the motive is still being investigated.
The commercial flight had 172 people on board, according to the airline, the majority of whom were Israeli. All passengers and crew were safe and accounted for after the plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. They were flown to Tel Aviv late Wednesday.
Investigators said that the co-pilot carried out the attack with what's called a crash axe — a lightweight emergency tool stored in the cockpit to break through panels or jammed doors in the event of a crash.
The aviation tracking site Flightradar24 said data shows at one point the plane descended more than 14,000 feet, or nearly 3 miles, in under 30 seconds — way faster than normal.
The pilot was able to open the cockpit door during the attack, and passengers rushed in and subdued the attacker, while another pilot who happened to be on board helped land the plane, according to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who spoke to the injured pilot as he was recovering in the hospital.
Both the pilot and the co-pilot are alive and have been transferred to the UAE for questioning.
The co-pilot is from Oman, according to Israeli officials. Omani and Emirati officials have not confirmed that publicly.
The detail of his nationality is raising questions in Israel about how he was allowed to fly a plane heading to Ben Gurion, as Israel does not allow pilots from countries it doesn't have diplomatic relations with to fly in its airspace. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Fox & Friends that Israel checks the background of pilots flying routes into the country, and that the attacker must have gotten through a "loophole."
Officials from Israel's Ministry of Transportation and security services have traded accusations over the lack of oversight and vetting of the pilot. Meanwhile, several of Netanyahu's political opponents have said the security breach is a failure on the prime minister's part and have called for a larger investigation.
Netanyahu announced late Sunday that there will be a formal examination into the security situation around "foreign civil aviation into Israel," but did not provide further details.
National elections in Israel — which will determine whether or not Netanyahu will remain prime minister — are just weeks away. It's the first such national election since the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, which sparked the war in Gaza.
Polls in Israel show that the race is tight, and analysts say the FlyDubai attack would likely not change Israelis' attitudes on how they will vote.
Netanyahu has been campaigning largely on the idea that he alone can protect Israelis from the external threats that Israel faces, while his opponents have pointed to what they see as major security failures under his leadership — including the Oct. 7 attack.

articles.title_orig: Trump heads to Nebraska to rescue GOP seat as his beef import plan angers rural voters
articles.title_zh: Trump heads to Nebraska to rescue GOP seat as his beef import plan angers rural voters
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump is taking his Republican midterm rescue mission to Nebraska on Monday, campaigning alongside GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts, who is running against an independent candidate backed by national Democrats .
Trump is headed to Grand Island, Nebraska, located in the solidly conservative south-central part of the state. It’s part of what the Republican president says is a 32-day blitz of rallies ahead of Nov. 3 that so far has taken him to ruby-red territory such as Oklahoma and Alabama . On Wednesday, he’ll make his second stop in two weeks in Texas with a rally in San Antonio.
“The president’s coming to Nebraska to help me campaign, so I can get reelected,” Ricketts told the Associated Press last week on Capitol Hill.
Ricketts, a former governor of the state, was appointed then later elected to fill Sen. Ben Sasse’s seat when he left to run the University of Florida in 2023. Now he is running for his first full six-year term against independent Dan Osborn — a race that initially was not expected to be competitive but is now being watched by the national parties.
Voters across the country are frustrated with Trump’s handling of the economy , including persistently high costs for fuel and groceries. It’s a major issue for rural voters who have backed the president and his party in recent elections.
The administration’s plan to allow more imports of foreign beef has particularly roiled the agriculture-rich state of Nebraska. Trump wants to lower beef prices for consumers, but ranchers have rebelled against the import proposal, arguing it would undercut them.
“The plan to import low-quality foreign beef is not helping Nebraska ranchers,” Ricketts told the AP. “I would advise the White House to change that policy and look for longer-term things that will help us build the size of the herd and ultimately bring the price of beef down for consumers.”
In the House of Representatives, the Grand Island area is represented by Republican Rep. Adrian Smith, whose race is not expected to be close. But Nebraska has a competitive House race farther east in Omaha , considered the “blue dot” of the state because the area’s electoral vote in presidential elections often goes to Democrats.
Osborn, a former labor union chief, ran against Republican Sen. Deb Fischer in 2024 and lost by 7 percentage points. Though national Democrats support him, he has refused to say what party he would caucus with should he be elected in November.
Other independents in the Senate, including Maine’s Angus King on the moderate end and Vermont’s Bernie Sanders on the left, caucus with Democrats for organizational purposes and committee assignments.
With the Democratic brand remaining deeply unpopular in conservative states, Osborn isn’t the only declared independent running for the Senate against Republicans this year. In South Dakota, Navy and Air Force veteran Brian Bengs is campaigning as an independent against Republican Sen. Mike Rounds. Bengs ran as a Democrat for the Senate four years ago and was handily defeated by now-Senate Majority Leader John Thune.
It’s a similar dynamic in Idaho, where independent Todd Achilles is challenging GOP Sen. Jim Risch.
Democratic voters in Nebraska chose Cindy Burbank as their party nominee earlier this year, but Burbank specifically campaigned on ensuring that no votes would be siphoned from Osborn in the general elections in November, and she has since formally dropped out of the race.
Osborn has been traveling across Nebraska to hold meetings in all 93 counties, and has repeatedly criticized Ricketts for not holding town halls to meet with constituents.
Ricketts, whose family founded TD Ameritrade and owns Major League Baseball’s Chicago Cubs, served as governor from 2015 to 2023.

With this in mind, we'll keep this article updated throughout the event, and keep an eye on the MacRumors front page as we'll be posting particularly great deals in separate articles this week.

articles.title_orig: Old World Christmas Turns the Holiday Favorite Royal Dansk® Cookie Tin Into a Glass Ornament
articles.title_zh: Old World Christmas Turns the Holiday Favorite Royal Dansk® Cookie Tin Into a Glass Ornament
articles.content_orig:
SPOKANE, Wash., Oct. 5, 2026
Old World Christmas has partnered with Royal Dansk ® to turn the Danish butter cookie tin into a hand-painted glass ornament, arriving just in time for the 2026 holiday season.
SPOKANE, Wash. , Oct. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- For 60 years, the Royal Dansk® blue tin has been part of holiday traditions around the world. First filled with Danish Butter Cookies, it often takes a second life storing buttons, thread, and family keepsakes. Now, that beloved blue tin has been reimagined. Old World Christmas , the premier brand of hand-crafted glass ornaments, has partnered with Royal Dansk to turn its iconic Danish Butter Cookie tin into a mouth-blown, hand-painted glass ornament. The Butter Cookies Tin Ornament is available this holiday season at OldWorldChristmas.com .
Why this partnership matters Few cookies are as recognizable as the iconic Royal Dansk blue tin. Often repurposed to hold sewing supplies and treasured mementos, the tin has earned a lasting place in homes for generations. That's the nostalgia and tradition this ornament celebrates.
Old World Christmas has spent more than 45 years turning everyday objects and cultural touchstones into collectible keepsakes. Pairing that craft with one of the most recognizable tins in the world gives shoppers a way to keep the memory out year-round, not just for the few weeks the cookies last.
"The Royal Dansk tin is already in millions of homes. We just made a version you can hang on the tree," said Neal Applefeld, President and CEO of Old World Christmas. "We love taking the everyday objects and traditions people recognize and turning them into keepsakes they can enjoy year after year."
"For generations, the Royal Dansk blue tin has been a cherished holiday tradition," said Kris Nance, Brand Manager at Royal Dansk. "We've heard countless stories about families sharing our butter cookies and then finding new uses for the tin long after the cookies were gone. Seeing this iconic symbol reimagined as a holiday ornament is a wonderful way to celebrate those memories and the joy of the season."
Frequently Asked Questions
What is the Old World Christmas Royal Dansk ornament? It's a hand-crafted glass Christmas ornament shaped after Royal Dansk's iconic blue Danish Butter Cookies tin. Old World Christmas mouth-blows and hand-paints each one.
Where can I buy the Royal Dansk ornament? The ornament is available at OldWorldChristmas.com and Amazon in time for the 2026 holiday season.
How much does the Royal Dansk ornament cost? $27.99
Why did Royal Dansk and Old World Christmas partner up? Royal Dansk's blue tin is one of the most recognizable cookie tins around, and Old World Christmas has made glass ornaments since 1979.  Together, they turned a 60-year cookie tradition into a collectible ornament, with plans to expand the partnership.
Is the ornament made of glass? Yes. Like all Old World Christmas ornaments, it's mouth-blown from molten glass and hand-painted, using techniques inspired by 19th-century ornament-making.
When is the best time to buy it as a gift? It's a nostalgic pick for the 2026 holidays and pairs naturally with National Cookie Day on December 4. Order early, since these special partnership hand-crafted holiday ornaments tend to sell out.
About Old World Christmas Old World Christmas has made hand-blown glass ornaments since 1979. Each design is created in-house and handcrafted by skilled artisans, and the collection now spans more than 2,000 proprietary designs, from traditional to whimsical. Built to last and made to capture a memory, a milestone, a pet, or a person you love, the ornaments give everyone a way to tell the story of their lives one piece at a time. Learn more at www.oldworldchristmas.com .
About Royal Dansk Royal Dansk® Danish Butter Cookies have been elegantly crafted in Denmark since 1966, honoring traditional Danish baking from their origins in Helsingør. Produced exclusively in the Danish bakeries of Nørre Snede and Ribe, the cookies are made with real butter and contain no preservatives or artificial ingredients, staying true to the brand's commitment to quality. Royal Dansk offers a signature variety of artisanal cookie shapes, always presented in the iconic blue packaging. Keep up with the latest news at www.royal-dansk.com and on Facebook and Instagram .
