articles.title_orig: Ukraine, U.S. Dominate U20 World Beach Wrestling
articles.title_zh: Ukraine, U.S. Dominate U20 World Beach Wrestling
articles.content_orig:
KATERINI, Greece (October 2) -- The U20 World Beach Wrestling Championships concluded in Katerini, Greece with Ukraine once again dominating the competition. A total of 95 wrestler representing 14 nations competed in four men's and four women's weight categories.
Ukraine finished top of podium in the men's team ranking with 75 points, ahead of Georgia on 55 points and Moldova on 52 points. Ukraine won two gold medals, at 90kg and +90kg.
At 70kg, Ionut TRIBOLI (MDA) produced the standout performance of the men's competition, going unbeaten throughout the tournament with seven victories before defeating Aik KAZARIAN (GRE), 2-1, in the final.
Georgia dominated the 80kg podium, with Luka MAKHARADZE (GEO) taking gold after blanking teammate Zurab MAMULADZE (GEO), 4-0, in the final. Makharadze did not conceded any points across his five wins.
Magor LORINCZ (ROU) finished with five victories to take the gold medal at 90kg after he won the final 3-0 over Samir IBISHOV (UKR). The results of the final +90kg division was reversed as Ruslan PROKOPOV (UKR) defeated Brian TECHEREAN (ROU) 3-0 in just 1:04 to claim the gold medal.
While it did not win any gold medals, the United States won the team title in women's beach wrestling with 53 points. Germany finished a close second with 52 points and Moldova managed the third position with 48 points.
Alevtyna LIASHENKO (UKR) won the 50kg gold medal after blanking Harua YAMAMOTO (JPN), 3-0, in the final to give Ukraine it's only title.
Milica PEROVIC (SRB) gave Serbia a rare gold after dominating the 60kg weight categories with seven victories and 23 technical points and did not concede a single point. She finished the 60kg final in just 20 seconds, securing a fall over Karolina POPLAVSKA (UKR).
Alexandra MOISEI (MDA) captured 70kg gold medal, narrowly edging Amber HUNTER (USA), 2-1, in the final bout. Mia BAUER (GER) gave Germany a gold medal in the +70kg category after edging Izabela KHUTSUSHVILI (GEO), 1-0, in the gold-medal bout.

articles.title_orig: ‘The future is bright’: breeding programme brings world’s heaviest insect back from the brink
articles.title_zh: ‘The future is bright’: breeding programme brings world’s heaviest insect back from the brink
articles.content_orig:
Wētāpunga can weigh as much as a mouse and its numbers dwindled across New Zealand due to predators and habitat loss
The population of New Zealand’s endemic wētāpunga – believed to be the world’s heaviest insect – is officially “recovering” thanks to a groundbreaking breeding programme that has overseen the release of 11,000 insects into the wild.
“The future of wētāpunga is looking bright,” said Dr Chris Green, an honorary researcher at the department of conservation, who documented the success of the project for the New Zealand Journal of Zoology. Green co-authored a report released on 2 October that outlines the success of the breeding programme.
“Eleven thousand individuals for release is extraordinary and outstanding.”
A female wētāpunga can weigh as much as a mouse. Its body can grow up to 10cm long (nearly 4in) and its leg span can be as wide as 20cm.
It is the largest of 70 wētā species and was once found across parts of the North Island before predation from introduced species and habitat loss contributed to their decline. By the 1990s, they were considered “endangered” and are now presumed extinct in the wild on New Zealand’s mainland. The insects reside primarily on a smattering of predator-free islands in Auckland’s Hauraki Gulf and off the coast of Northland.
But their fortune is starting to change. Over the past 15 years, tens of thousands of wētāpunga have been bred at Butterfly Creek, a wildlife facility, and Auckland zoo, enabling the release of wētāpunga across new predator-free islands and some mainland reserves north of Auckland.
Butterfly Creek and Auckland zoo established husbandry techniques that, over time, have been scaled up to rear large numbers of wētāpunga in communal creches. The young wētāpunga – or nymphs – are fed a three-part diet of fresh foliage, fish flake protein and leaf litter. The protein is “critical” to the survival of the youngest nymphs, Green said.
Once big enough to protect themselves, the insects are transferred to their new habitat. The efforts have led to 45 separate translocations to wild habitats, which is “a very high number in any recovery of a species”, Green said.
Monitoring on two islands has shown wētāpunga have established self-sustaining populations, with fourth and fifth generations born there, in what Green said was a marker of success. As a result, the species’ conservation status has improved from “nationally endangered” to “nationally recovering”.
“It’s so exciting, because we are unable to report that for so many of our other threatened species,” Green said.
New Zealand is particularly vulnerable to species decline because of its high rates of endemism and problems with introduced pests.
Green said the country was at the forefront of invertebrate recovery work and he was not aware of any other examples of breeding programmes working to this scale, or with such success.
By documenting the project’s work, he hopes other institutions will feel encouraged to develop their own programmes.
“That’s the extraordinary aspect of it – that we’ve been successful,” he said. “If other institutions can get into that sort of position, then there can be huge benefit for threatened species in New Zealand.”

articles.title_orig: GM says hybrid vehicles are coming: 'We're not tone deaf to our customers'
articles.title_zh: GM says hybrid vehicles are coming: 'We're not tone deaf to our customers'
articles.content_orig:
DETROIT — General Motors plans to introduce hybrid models into its U.S. lineup as sales of the vehicles continue to grow amid inflated gas prices and a pullback in all-electric cars.
Mike Anderson, GM's vice president of propulsion engineering, reconfirmed the automaker's hybrid plans, but declined to discuss timing for such vehicles, which had previously been expected as soon as next year.
"It's fair to say that [hybrids are] part of the plan," Anderson, a 35-year GM veteran, told CNBC during an interview. "We're not tone deaf to our customers. We know what they want and we want to give that to them as quickly as we can."
GM has largely been absent from the hybrid market this decade, instead using its resources to go "all-in" on all-electric vehicles . But amid lackluster EV demand, industry deregulation and increased hybrid popularity, Anderson said the company needs to meet customer demand wherever it may be.
"Our long-term vision is an all-electric future. That's our goal," Anderson said. "That's the end state, but it's going to be a journey that involves technology diversity."
GM CEO Mary Barra in January said the automaker was still studying plug-in hybrid electric vehicles, or PHEVs, for its U.S. lineup as well as traditional hybrids but remained critical of the technologies. She also told Bloomberg later that month that a "handful" of such models were coming but did not give a timeline.
In mid-2024, GM announced plans to introduce PHEVs by 2027. At that time, GM was under pressure to meet stricter federal tailpipe emissions standards that have since been lowered or eliminated by the Trump administration.
AutoForecast Solutions, an automotive data and consulting firm, expects GM to begin offering PHEVs in late 2027 to early 2028 with a 70-mile EV range "throughout its portfolio," according to Casey Selecman, director of powertrain forecasts for the company.
"GM has several PHEVs planned throughout the portfolio from the Equinox to the Silverado but has been very cautious in rolling them out due to fears of customer technology preference changes that have burned them in the past," he said.
Anderson declined to discuss potential products or timing for GM's first new hybrid model.
"You can see, without me saying what our future plans are, where the customers are clamoring for these things and really, really going for them," he said. "We want to meet them where they want things."
Sales of hybrid models in the U.S. have jumped amid dimming EV demand, inflated gas prices and more offerings in the market, which GM has been missing out on.
Cox Automotive reports hybrid vehicle sales from the second quarter of this year increased 23% from a year earlier to represent a record 16.3% of U.S. sales from April through June. That compares with roughly 5.8% of sales for EVs, Cox said.
There are a growing number of hybrid variants being introduced by automakers but, in general, those vehicles combine a traditional gas-powered engine with electric motors and a battery to offer better fuel economy and, in many cases, better performance.
The fastest-growing segments for hybrids in the U.S. are compact crossover/SUV and mid-size vehicles, according to Cox.
"Hybrid vehicles continue to be the clearest growth story in the electrified market," Stephanie Valdez Streaty, Cox director of industry insights, said during a presentation last week.
There are currently a few types of hybrids available in the U.S. Traditional hybrids, like a Toyota Prius, feature many electrified engine technologies, while PHEVs have a designated all-electric range before using an engine to power the vehicle.
Then there are extended-range electric vehicles, or "series hybrids," that drive like an EV but have an engine that essentially operates like a generator to power electric motors to propel a vehicle.
The combination of two powertrains adds additional complexity and costs, which has been an argument GM has made against hybrids, but it's something many consumers appear willing to pay for as hybrid sales continue to rise.
GM currently offers only one hybrid, a model of its Chevrolet Corvette. The Detroit automaker's last true push into hybrids was the Chevrolet Volt plug-in , which was discontinued in 2019.
GM's crosstown rivals, Ford Motor and Chrysler parent Stellantis , have leaned on suppliers to get hybrid vehicles to market more quickly.
Anderson said GM's strategy "will be a mix" of internal and external technologies based on cost, segment and product.
"We're deliberate because, usually for strategic reasons, we need to control our own destiny. We need to control our own timing," he said. "Or, if it's commodity, go get it. Go get the best price you can."

articles.title_orig: Cornell student who gave police leads in alleged rape says she feels ‘betrayed’ over its handling
articles.title_zh: Cornell student who gave police leads in alleged rape says she feels ‘betrayed’ over its handling
articles.content_orig:
A Cornell University student gave campus police leads in the alleged rape of Jane Doe in 2024 but expressed dismay over how the authorities handled the case.
The student, who spoke to NBC News on Sunday on condition of anonymity over concerns about repercussions, said she first heard about allegations that Doe was raped as a rumor on campus about 24 to 48 hours after the incident. Doe, who filed a lawsuit last month, claimed she was plied with alcohol and ketamine and gang-raped at the Chi Phi fraternity house the night of Oct. 19-20.
The student recalled rumors that Doe was planning to have a threesome but that it had “gone off the rails,” and she remembers being “really horrified by it.”
“From that night, I think, we just kind of started, like, hearing more,” the student said.
Talk of the alleged sexual assault became widespread on campus after the school issued a crime safety alert about a report of a sexual assault at a fraternity.
“The thing I think we all feel, like, betrayed in regards to is that, like, it wasn’t handled,” she said. “When we got the police report, I think we all assumed it was being, you know, it would be, like, handled properly, yeah, and it was, like, in good hands.”
The student, who discussed details corroborated by documents reviewed by NBC News, said she and a friend initially gave a tip to authorities after the crime alert was issued. Police later called her and asked her to come in and speak with them days after Doe reported the incident to Cornell police on Nov. 8.
The student said she decided to go to police after she saw screenshots of a Chi Phi group message on Snapchat and because “it felt like the right thing to do if we could help this girl.” Doe’s lawsuit included a screenshot of a Chi Phi Snapchat group message that said there was “free p----” in a room in the frat house where Doe was the night she alleges she was assaulted.
“That was, like, when I kind of internally made the decision. OK, like, I’m taking this all in, and then I’m going to the police tomorrow,” the student said.
She recalled sitting with one or two officers for about half an hour during her interview with police.
“They seemed fairly competent. It seemed like a normal interview process to me,” she said.
She said she walked them through everything she knew, including that fraternity members were messaging about the events of that evening with Doe and about potential witnesses. She also gave police secondhand information about drug use at Chi Phi and said she is familiar with the frat house and believed she knew where ketamine was alleged to be kept.
“I guess I assumed that, like, I wasn’t enough,” the student said.
Cornell did not immediately respond to a request for comment Sunday on the student’s account to police. In a video statement Saturday, President Michael I. Kotlikoff called the allegations “deeply disturbing” and said they raise questions about the investigations that were conducted. He said he welcomes an independent review of how the university handled the matter, which will be conducted by an outside law firm.
Police records obtained by NBC News showed that Cornell police spoke to multiple witnesses and fielded anonymous tips about the allegations of a gang rape at the fraternity house — but that the information was not referred to the local prosecutor for review in his deciding whether to bring charges.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten told NBC News on Friday that the interviews that were flagged “were each of the frat members declining to speak on the advice of their attorney.” He did not respond to a follow-up request asking whether he was told about interviews with other fraternity members in addition to tips from callers.
Van Houten ultimately determined the allegations did not warrant charges because of a lack of criminality.
Doe’s suit has sparked uproar and criticism of Cornell and Van Houten’s handling of her allegations. Van Houten has since agreed to reopen his inquiry into Doe’s allegations, but New York Gov. Kathy Hochul last week named state Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor in the matter.
The student who spoke with campus police criticized how the department handled the matter. While students believed there was an active investigation into Doe’s claims, people continued going to Chi Phi, including the room at the center of the allegations.
Within Greek life at Cornell, “rumors spread fast,” the student said, and even if you did not know Doe or the men, “you knew someone who did.”
Doe’s lawsuit named Cornell, Chi Phi and the seven fraternity brothers among the defendants. None of the seven has been criminally charged. The fraternity was suspended from campus, and it remains barred.
Cornell said in a statement on Sept. 28 that it conducted a thorough, monthslong Title IX investigation that handed down “a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions ” from the university.
According to a source who has seen the written decision of the Title IX investigation, two of the fraternity members were expelled, and another two were suspected. A third, who had already graduated, was barred from campus, and the final two were issued no-contact orders and “reflection papers.”
Attorneys for two of the seven men have denied to NBC News that they sexually assaulted Doe. An attorney for a third man denied the allegations to ABC News. NBC News has not received responses to requests for comment from the five other men.
Chi Phi’s national fraternity condemned sexual assault and drug and alcohol abuse in a statement Wednesday. It said that the fraternity members Doe named were kicked out of the organization and that the national fraternity permanently expelled the chapter.
“At every level of Chi Phi, we will take steps like these whenever they are needed to protect the integrity of our fraternity and the safety of our communities,” said Trey Robb, the national fraternity’s interim executive director.
Some of the men faced backlash as talk spread on campus.
Two of the Chi Phi brothers named in the suit were kicked out of their rugby club after the allegations came to light, a former teammate told NBC News.
“We kicked [them] off the team immediately before the school expelled them,” said the teammate, who requested anonymity because of the sensitivity of the matter.
The teammate said he has participated in discussions among a group of current and former rugby players about responding publicly to Doe’s lawsuit.
“As a team, it was important for us to support this victim,” he said. “We are extremely, extremely distraught.”
Cornell Rugby said in a statement that it was “deeply disturbed” by the allegations and that its thoughts were with Doe.
“Players who were known to be connected with the alleged events were permanently removed from the team and alumni network as soon as their affiliation with the incident was established,” it said.
No current members of the team have been affiliated with Chi Phi, the statement said.
As news of the allegations spread, some discussions were supportive of Doe, but others shamed her in conversations, a former member of Doe’s sorority, Delta Delta Delta, told NBC News.
“Some people were sympathizing with Jane Doe, but also, people didn’t know details,” said the former member, who has graduated and requested anonymity out of a concern for privacy.
Another student and former member of Tri Delta told NBC News that she recalled learning about the incident through rumors and described the student body as “really pissed off about it.”
That student said that she was at the same sorority-hosted event the evening of Oct. 19 that Doe attended and which was referred to in her lawsuit but that Doe disappeared during the evening.
A few days later, the student said, Doe said people were spreading rumors about her and she was not sure what to make of it, “and it just seemed like everybody was very confused at the moment.”

articles.title_orig: Clemson scientist helps reveal a largely hidden world of giant viruses
articles.title_zh: Clemson scientist helps reveal a largely hidden world of giant viruses
articles.content_orig:
When we think of viruses, we often associate them with disease, but many viruses in nature have nothing to do with human illness.
A new study that included Clemson University microbiologist Barbara Campbell suggests that one poorly described group in particular — giant viruses — may be important participants in ecosystems ranging from ocean and freshwater systems to soil.
A collaborative international research team created the largest catalog yet of giant virus genomes. The collection includes 18,727 metagenome-assembled genomes, which are genetic reconstructions made from environmental samples from marine and freshwater systems, soil, rock, thermal springs, plant-associated environments and landfills.
After comparing the genomes, the researchers identified 8,508 species-level representatives, 712 previously unknown genera, 13 new viral families and a proposed new order called Mycodnavirales .
The study, published in the journal Nature Microbiology, provides new clues about the diversity and possible ecological roles of giant viruses.
“We’re interested in what’s going on out there in the environment at the microbial scale,” said Campbell, much of whose research involves the Chesapeake and Delaware bays .  Her group is especially interested in the ecological questions of “Who’s there? What are they doing? What and who are they interacting with?”
The study uses metagenomics to help answer those questions.
Most of the microbes in marine and estuarine environments are difficult to grow in the laboratory, and studying viruses depends on host cells. With metagenomics, scientists collect an environmental sample and sequence all the DNA in it. The genetic material comes from many organisms, and researchers use bioinformatic tools on high-performance computers such as Palmetto to assemble the fragments into larger sequences that can reveal the organisms’ identities.
“It allows us to look to see what’s in the environment without actually having to culture it,” Campbell said.
Despite their name, giant viruses can’t be seen by the human eye.
“They are giant, but giant is relative,” Campbell said. “You still need a microscope to see them.”
Bacteria are huge when compared to viruses. The smallest bacteria are about 0.4 microns in diameter, or one millionth of a meter. Viruses range in size from 0.02 to 0.25 microns. Most viruses are submicroscopic, meaning they are unable to be seen in an ordinary light microscope. They are typically studied with an electron microscope.
But some giant viruses are nearly the size of bacteria, and their genomes can exceed 2.5 million DNA base pairs. They may have hundreds of thousands of genes, including genes related to metabolism and protein production. That genetic complexity gives giant viruses the potential to influence the cells they infect in unusual ways.
Some giant viruses carry genes associated with producing proteins, a process other viruses leave to their hosts. Others contain genes connected to metabolism, stress responses and cell signaling.
“A lot of them have most everything needed to sustain life,” Campbell said.
That doesn’t mean they live independently. They still need host cells to reproduce. But their large genomes may allow them to manipulate host cells in more complicated ways than smaller viruses can.
According to the study, researchers found potential clues about the environmental roles of giant viruses, too. For instance, some groups contained genes associated with processing formaldehyde and breaking down aromatic compounds, including substances that can occur in industrial pollution.
The giant viruses in the study are generally host-specific and are not expected to infect humans. However, their impact could be felt by humans because they may help shape the health of oceans, bays, lakes and soil.
For Campbell, the results reinforce how much scientists still do not know about the smallest life forms in oceans and estuarine waters.
Viruses are part of what scientists call the microbial loop. Many giant viruses infect microscopic organisms such as phytoplankton and protists. When viruses break open their hosts, nutrients inside the cells are released back into the environment where they can be used by other organisms.
In low-nutrient marine and estuarine environments, that recycling can be especially important. Estuarine and marine phytoplankton are essentially single-celled plants that absorb carbon dioxide and produce roughly half the Earth’s oxygen she said.
“So knowing more about what makes them tick, and how they survive and die, is important, and studies like this give us an excellent starting point,” Campbell said.

articles.title_orig: Catholic schools, banned rifles and ‘climate lawfare’: Blockbuster fights await Supreme Court
articles.title_zh: Catholic schools, banned rifles and ‘climate lawfare’: Blockbuster fights await Supreme Court
articles.content_orig:
Supreme Court justices will begin hearing oral arguments Monday on a wide range of cases this term involving gun rights, religious freedom, immigration detention and the limits of government power.
The Supreme Court opens its new term Monday with cases that could reshape religious liberty, gun rights, immigration and the balance between state and federal authority.
While the last term was dominated by major cases testing presidential power — including Trump’s authority to restrict birthright citizenship, impose tariffs and fire independent agency officials — many of the court’s marquee cases this term span a wide range of issues, including federalism and individual rights.
"There’s a couple of religious freedom cases," Carrie Severino, president of JCN, told Fox News Digital. "We have a couple cases that touch on state and federal preemption, but I’m not sure there’s an easy theme for all of them."
The blockbuster case this term is Suncor Energy v. Boulder County, and it centers on whether Colorado officials can use state tort law to seek damages from oil giants Suncor and ExxonMobil for climate-related harms, or whether federal law blocks those claims.
The Supreme Court opens its new term Monday with major cases involving executive power, gun rights, religious liberty and voting rules. (Photo by Leah Millis-Pool/Getty Images)
SUPREME COURT CLIMATE SHOWDOWN JOLTED BY ALITO'S LAST-MINUTE DECISION
"If Colorado actually succeeds on its nuisance claims and others against these companies, the upshot would not just be these companies changing what they do in a way to protect Colorado or remedy Colorado, but rather it would affect their operations far outside of the state," Adam White, senior fellow at American Enterprise Institute, shared during a Federalist Society Panel. "And the question is, can Colorado courts reach outside of their own state and try in effect to regulate?"
Suncor and ExxonMobil argue that the Clean Air Act gives the federal government authority over interstate and international emissions, leaving Colorado unable to hold them liable for conduct outside the state. But the state argues that it is seeking damages under state law and that the Clean Air Act preserves states’ authority to enforce their own laws.
The Supreme Court will decide whether federal law blocks Boulder’s climate lawsuit and whether the justices can hear the case.
Severino said the case is an effort by "climate lawfare activists" to regulate carbon emissions.
"If the court is viewing this as an effort to weaponize one jurisdiction's law to really regulate outside its borders, then I think they're going to be not very happy about this claim," Severino said. "If the court really views it as an attempt by Colorado to legislate worldwide actions of these energy companies, then I think they're going to say this is actually something that fits within the federal government's sphere of activity, not a single state."
The case marks the first oral arguments heard before the high court.
An Arizona election integrity measure is at the center of another Supreme Court case testing the balance of power between states and the federal government over how elections are run.
Smith & Wesson M&P-15 semi-automatic rifles of the AR-15 style are displayed during the National Rifle Association (NRA) annual meeting at the George R. Brown Convention Center, in Houston, Texas, on May 28, 2022. (PATRICK T. FALLON/AFP via Getty Images)
THESE 11 UPCOMING SUPREME COURT DECISIONS COULD MAKE OR BREAK TRUMP'S SECOND TERM AGENDA
Republican National Committee v. Mi Familia Vota stems from an Arizona law requiring documentary proof of U.S. citizenship for certain voter registrations. Voters who register without that documentation may qualify as "federal-only" voters, allowing them to vote in federal elections but not state and local races. The law also allows the state to purge noncitizens off voter rolls close to an election. The dispute centers on whether the National Voter Registration Act prevents Arizona from imposing additional requirements on voters.
The Supreme Court will also hear major cases involving gun rights and religious liberty and will determine how far states can go in limiting those freedoms.
Colorado is up to bat twice before the Supreme Court this term, with St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy testing whether the state can exclude Catholic preschools from its universal preschool program because of religious policies barring same-sex couples and LGBT students from attending the schools, which conflicts with the state’s nondiscrimination requirements.
Colorado provides funding to private preschools that participate in the program but requires them to follow state anti-discrimination rules covering sexual orientation and gender identity. The Catholic schools argue those rules clash with their religious beliefs and that they should not have to abandon their policies to receive the same funding available to other private schools.
"They don't agree with the state on things like allowing children to use the opposite sex bathroom if they identify with the opposite sex. So this is something the Supreme Court has been very favorable to religious organizations of and for not allowing states to just cut them out of otherwise generally applicable state benefit programs," Severino said.
The U.S. Supreme Court cleared the way for the Trump administration to continue third-world country deportations while the justices consider a legal challenge to the policy. (Getty Images)
EXCLUSIVE: SUPREME COURT PRAYER GROTTO CASE COULD IMPACT 'EVERY SINGLE ZONING LAW' IN AMERICA, ATTORNEY SAYS
But Amanda Shanor, an attorney who helped represent the gay couple who were denied a wedding cake before the Supreme Court, said during a Federalist Society Panel there is concern that the case could chip away at anti-discrimination protections by expanding when businesses and institutions can refuse to serve people based on their identity.
"The schools are not saying, like in the earlier cases — like Masterpiece Cake Shop or 303 Creative — that they want to not serve somebody because of the expression that it would express with regard to a particular event, but instead that they don’t want to have the kids or the families because of the status of the kids or the families," Shanor said. "And will that then go spread over into other things, like will the bakery be able to say, ‘I don’t want to serve all X type of people?’"
Illinois and Connecticut have cases, with state laws restricting certain semiautomatic firearms facing challenges at the Supreme Court.
Members of the Supreme Court pose for a group photo at the Supreme Court on Oct. 7, 2022. Seated from left: Associate Justice Sonia Sotomayor, Associate Justice Clarence Thomas, Chief Justice of the United States John G. Roberts Jr., Associate Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. and Associate Justice Elena Kagan. Standing behind from left: Associate Justice Amy Coney Barrett, Associate Justice Neil M. Gorsuch, Associate Justice Brett M. Kavanaugh and Associate Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)
"This is important because the Supreme Court, for the first time following its landmark Bruen decision, is going to be looking at how states or municipalities can limit particular types of weapons," Severino said. "What the court said it's going to look at is whether these are weapons that are in common use and have lawful purposes, and so this is the court's opportunity to look at things like the popular AR-15 type rifle and decide is this something that qualifies as something that's in common-use and therefore is protected by the Second Amendment."
And while presidential power may not be a major theme this term, the Supreme Court will still weigh the limits of the Trump administration’s authority in a case involving its push to deport illegal immigrants to third-world countries they are not from, and that are not listed in their removal orders.

articles.title_orig: Qalo SL-1 Review: A Barebones Smart Band That's Priced Like A Flagship
articles.title_zh: Qalo SL-1 Review: A Barebones Smart Band That's Priced Like A Flagship
articles.content_orig:
It’s the same price as the Garmin Cirqa.
I've already made my feelings about screenless fitness trackers well known to everyone who'll listen. They're more about signaling to the in-crowd that you're a serious gym goer than a better alternative to a proper smartwatch. Still, that's a big enough market that plenty of companies are jostling for space alongside Whoop (and Fitbit, and Garmin). Take Qalo, a jewelry brand with a side hustle selling smart rings, which is now branching out with its own screenless band. The Qalo SL-1 is a subscription-free band which aggregates all of your vital signs into a single score.
If you're unfamiliar, Qalo sells silicon rings for folks who, for many reasons, can't or won't wear a metal ring. If you work in heavy industry, it's wise to swap your wedding band for something that won't cause you to lose a finger in an accident. They're also a great option for the gym or other physical activities, as well as for folks who experience finger-swelling.
Qalo has launched two generations of rings in the last few years, with some corners of the internet saying they're re-branded hardware from J-Style, a white-label wearables manufacturer. A representative of the company told me that the SL-1 , however, is "built around QALO's own software, data and design."
It's worth understanding that if you own a Qalo smart ring, the SL-1 is complimentary with the rest of its ecosystem. So if you wear a ring during the day, but take it off for the gym, you can strap the band on your wrist or bicep and all of the data will aggregate to the same place.
At $199.95, Qalo is asking for the same sort of money as Garmin wants for its own smart band, the Cirqa . Which means there's an easy benchmark to see if this generic, first-generation hardware is capable of outperforming a wearables specialist with decades of experience.
The Qalo SL-1 is a screenless fitness tracker which looks like someone described a Whoop over the phone. It's a little longer than a Whoop MG but, to my eye, has a more pronounced bend in its chassis, although that didn't seem to affect how it sat on my wrist. Take it out of the box and you'll first notice the silicon strap, which attaches to itself magnetically.
In that initial moment, the idea of a magnetically-attached watch strap looks and sounds like the coolest idea imaginable. It'll take you all of 30 seconds to realize why other watchmakers don't do the same thing with their own products. Because, as elegant as the magnetic strap is, it will get easily dislodged if your sleeve slides along at the wrong angle.
Qalo says the water-resistant band lasts for 12 days on a single charge, and will keep an eye on the usual set of vital signs. That includes activity, sleep, heart rate, SpO2, HRV, stress, temperature and menstrual cycle tracking. It ships with a magnetic USB-C charging cradle which I would describe as heavy for what it is.
Like the devices it's competing with, the SL-1 collects a trove of data about you, but knows it's too much for you to take in. Consequently, it produces a Q Score, a single 1-100 metric telling you how well you're looking after yourself and how much fuel is in your tank. As you can see from the screenshot, the score is joined by three other metrics: Sleep, Movement, and Vitality. The latter aggregates your resting heart rate, resting HRV, blood oxygenation level and skin temperature.
Open the app each morning, and you'll get a pop-up telling you your Q Score for the previous day. Get enough sleep and exercise, and that figure will be high, and if you look after yourself for several days in a row, you'll get a streak encouraging you to keep it going.
Once dismissed, you'll be able to look at the home screen, which provides live updates on Q Score throughout the day. Annoyingly, its conclusions exist in a vacuum, and are written past-tense. Look at this first thing in the morning and you'll be told your score is low because you didn't log a workout and didn't walk enough. It's not a big deal in and of itself, unless you're really sensitive to being demoralized by your fitness wearable. But it's a sign the system does little beyond aggregating the data it's given, ignoring the broader context.
I'm also disappointed at the lack of automatic workout detection, at least for the basics, which should be a standard feature for any fitness band. The fact the SL-1 can't identify when I'm out for a walk and log that separately vexes, especially given the likelihood I'll forget to activate a workout. This omission may be easier to take if you couldn't get a product like Garmin's Cirqa for the same amount of money, which can do this.
Start an activity, and you'll get details on your heart rate zones, maximum and average HR, steps and calories burned. You'll even get your live heart rate and the zone you're in as a live activity on your phone's lock screen. You'll then get a breakdown of your heart rate zones and calories burned at the end of a workout, again much like you'll find on other devices.
One thing I cannot fault the SL-1 for is its battery life, and I suspect it'll make it at least past its 12-day promise. I've worn this thing a full week, and the battery is still reporting a charge level of 59 percent, which is worthy of praise in and of itself.
One of the hard things about testing the Qalo SL-1 was the fact I don't think it did anything well enough to outperform its rivals. There's no single killer feature it offers that would compel me to recommend it over any other screenless fitness tracker out there. Instead, it feels like the unit you'd recommend to someone who simply wanted to dip a toe into this market. It's basic, simple, commitment-free and achieves its laudable if unexciting goal of ticking all of the boxes.
But this device costs the same as a Garmin Cirqa , a device I didn't think was all that amazing, but did a lot of these basics better. The Cirqa is at least equipped with the fundamentals you'd expect from a company of Garmin's size and experience. Take automatic activity tracking, for example, which I'd say isn't just nice to have but an essential feature for even those of us who are sub-weekend warriors.
If the SL-1 was cheaper, I'd have more positive things to say about it, because you could easily see it as a My First Whoop . But for this sort of money, I'd say there are better alternatives, even when you factor in additional subscription fees.

articles.title_orig: Irvine woman detained while trying to fly to China, accused of surveilling in Seattle
articles.title_zh: Irvine woman detained while trying to fly to China, accused of surveilling in Seattle
articles.content_orig:
The FBI ⁠arrested Wanying Zhang, also known as Heather, at Los Angeles International Airport before she left for China, the agency said
US authorities arrested a California ⁠woman on ​Sunday, accusing her of spying on the son of Taiwan’s president at the behest of Chinese officials, the FBI said.
The FBI ⁠arrested Wanying Zhang, also known as Heather, at Los Angeles International Airport on Sunday before her planned departure to China , the agency said in a ⁠statement. Authorities charged Zhang, 34, of Irvine, California, with acting as an unregistered foreign agent.
Zhang surveilled a ​son of Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te, the ‌FBI alleged. The agency ‌did not directly name Zhang’s alleged target, but later shared a New York Post report ‌identifying him as Lai Ting-yu, a US resident.
Taiwan’s presidential office described Zhang’s alleged actions as a “typical case of transnational repression” and thanked the US government for protecting Taiwanese citizens.
“Our country expresses the strongest condemnation of such barbaric conduct that disregards human rights and the sovereignty of nations,” spokesperson Karen Kuo said in a statement.
China’s foreign ministry did not respond to ‌a request for comment.
The Justice Department alleged Zhang travelled to Seattle in 2025 at the direction of Chinese officials and sent them photos, video and licence plate information of the Taiwanese president’s son and his family.
Zhang used tradecraft to avoid detection ⁠and never notified Washington that she was acting for a foreign government, Bill Essayli, ​the first assistant US ​attorney for the Central District of ​California, alleged in a statement.
It was not immediately clear whether Zhang ​had a defence attorney. She ‌will appear on ​Monday in a ​Los Angeles federal court, Essayli said.
Lai and his Democratic Progressive Party champion Taiwan’s separate identity from China, a position that frequently angers Beijing, which views the island as ​Chinese territory. Lai says only Taiwan’s people can decide their future.
Washington does not have formal diplomatic ties with Taiwan, but the US is the island’s most important international backer and weapons supplier.

articles.title_orig: Spain Election Live Updates: Sánchez Calls for Nov. 29 Snap Election After Housing Crisis Roils Government
articles.title_zh: Spain Election Live Updates: Sánchez Calls for Nov. 29 Snap Election After Housing Crisis Roils Government
articles.content_orig:
SÃ¡nchez's announcement comes after a series of measures to tackle the housing crisis was defeated in parliament on Friday
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez has called an early election for 29 November after recent defeats on legislation aimed at addressing the country's housing crisis.
Speculation about a snap election had been building over the weekend after parliament rejected two decree laws put forward by the minority government to protect tenants in the rental market.
The eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home after she was unable to afford a sharp rent rise has sparked nationwide protests and increased pressure for housing reform.
In a televised address on Monday, SÃ¡nchez said that to push reforms through he needed "a broader progressive majority" that can "overcome the resistance of the elites".
Housing has not been the only issue causing problems for SÃ¡nchez's leadership in recent months, with his party having been caught up in numerous corruption scandals and facing pressure on other cost-of-living issues and immigration.
"We have made mistakes and have not achieved everything we had set out to do," SÃ¡nchez said, acknowledging there were still "a lot of problems to solve, particularly in the areas of inequality, of public services and access to housing".
SÃ¡nchez's left-wing coalition government is made up of his ruling Socialist party and junior partner the Sumar alliance, and does not have a majority in parliament.
Spain was not due to hold a general election until the summer of 2027 at the latest.
Spanish prime minister calls snap election after housing protests
SÃ¡nchez has been prime minister since June 2018. His Socialist party finished second in the last election, in 2023.
Although the conservative People's Party won the most seats, it fell short of a majority.
SÃ¡nchez remained in power after striking agreements with left-wing parties and securing support from Catalan and Basque nationalist and pro-independence groups.
Most opinion polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next election. However, they would be expected to need the support of the hard-right Vox party to form a government.
Speaking after Monday's announcement, the leader of the People's Party, Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o, said: "At last, Spaniards will be able to decide".
The opposition leader said it would not be "just another election", but a chance for voters to choose between "decline or change, lies or change, incompetence or change, division or change, corruption or change".
The eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from her Madrid home led to public outcry
On Saturday, tens of thousands of people took to the streets in cities including Madrid, Valencia and Barcelona, calling for greater protections for tenants.
Maricarmen Abascal, 87, became a symbol of Spain's housing crisis when she was forcibly evicted from her Madrid home on 23 September.
A legal glitch allowed her landlord to raise her rent from â¬500 (Â£428; $572) to â¬2,650. It was later lowered to â¬1,650 - still â¬300 more than her monthly pension.
She was removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years, and was later admitted to hospital.
Protests over housing took place in Madrid on Saturday
Her lawyer has since said she will be able to return to her home , but the incident has prompted widespread anger over housing.
The left-wing coalition government responded with two decree laws in an effort to defuse the protests.
The first included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by what the government calls "vulture funds".
The second decree was more controversial, because it included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the tenants' organisation Sindicato de Inquilinas.
The political right argued the government's attempt to intervene in the housing market would have led to fewer homes being rented and would have raised prices further.
Juan Bravo of the People's Party said last week "housing doesn't get cheaper with decrees, it gets cheaper with more homes".
The Spanish prime minister currently doesn't command a congressional majority
SÃ¡nchez's leadership has been marred by numerous corruption scandals in recent months.
In April, his wife BegoÃ±a GÃ³mez was charged with corruption after a two-year criminal investigation.
She is accused of using her relationship to advance her private career - allegations she denies, and which have been dismissed by SÃ¡nchez as a right-wing attempt to undermine his coalition.
In May, police raided the Socialist party's headquarters in Madrid as part of an investigation into allegations an operative was paid to carry out a misinformation campaign. The party has denied the allegations.
And in June, SÃ¡nchez's former transport minister, JosÃ© Luis Ãbalos, was jailed for 24 years after he was found guilty of being involved in a network that received kickbacks from the sale of face masks during the Covid-19 pandemic.
The Spanish prime minister also came under scrutiny for his handling of the Ceuta migration crisis over the summer, when tens of thousands of people entered the territory from Morocco without authorisation.

articles.title_orig: 'They'd never seen a car or a TV': The people evacuated to the UK from the world's most remote inhabited island in 1961
articles.title_zh: 'They'd never seen a car or a TV': The people evacuated to the UK from the world's most remote inhabited island in 1961
articles.content_orig:
After a volcano erupted on tiny Tristan da Cunha in the South Atlantic, the 264 displaced islanders told the BBC about their first taste of modern British life.
"Just over a year ago, they'd never seen traffic or a road or a house higher than a cottage," said Tim Brinton in a 1963 BBC programme. He was talking about the residents of Tristan da Cunha, the world's most remote inhabited island. In the middle of the South Atlantic Ocean, roughly halfway between Cape Town in South Africa and Rio de Janeiro in Brazil, the tiny British outpost is more than 1,500 miles from any other populated land, and is only accessible by a seven-day boat journey.
But on 10 October 1961, a sudden volcanic eruption blasted the islanders out of their splendid isolation and into the industrialised modern world. "We heard the rumbles first, then the ground just automatically cracked… Then the smoke and the fire started coming out the ground," one of them told the BBC in a 1998 film. Another, Mary Swain, said that she'd run to her husband and shouted, "Jump up quick, Fred, the Earth is opening!"
The island's volcano had been dormant since Tristan was first settled 150 years earlier. But great cracks appeared in the ground a few hundred metres from the main village, which is named Edinburgh of the Seven Seas. By the time the islanders had escaped in their fishing boats to nearby Nightingale Island, their homes were already threatened by lava. "The whole place is vibrating with earthquakes," announced a BBC reporter, "and the eastern corner is cracking and breaking up."
Tristan's 264 inhabitants were forced to evacuate , picked up by a Dutch liner that happened to arrive the next day. Within hours, the whole community was aboard, leaving everything apart from the few things they could carry with them – "a rifle, an overcoat and a lamp," recalled Swain – and their boats, which they stored in their gardens when they reached England weeks later.
They were housed on a disused military airbase near Southampton, a port city on England's south coast. "So much is strange to them," said Brinton. "They'd never seen shops because on the island, money wasn't used. Boats were their livelihood. For them, there's been no industrial revolution. And for 150 years, they've lived simple agricultural lives out of touch with world progress."
Though Tristan da Cunha was discovered in 1506 by a Portuguese admiral who gave it his name, it was another 300 years before it supported anything but seabirds and seals. The UK annexed the island in 1816 to prevent it being used as a base for attempts to free Napoleon Bonaparte from his imprisonment on the South Atlantic island of St Helena . The following year, a Scotsman, Corporal William Glass, stayed behind when the British garrison was withdrawn. With his family and a few others, he founded the first permanent community.
In History is a series which uses the BBC's unique audio and video archive to explore historical events that still resonate today. Sign up to the accompanying weekly newsletter.
By 1961, the population of the 40 sq miles (100 sq km) of volcanic rock had risen to 264, many of them survivors from ships wrecked on the island, with just seven family names between them. On several occasions, the failure of the potato crop or the wrecking of fishing boats brought the islanders to the point of starvation. But they stayed on, even defying several attempts by the British government to evacuate them.
When the volcanic eruption forced the islanders to leave, they faced difficulties settling in England. They had never seen a car, a bicycle, a TV set or an income tax form. And it was a challenging climate. "Here is too much gas and smoke," Tristanian Joey Repetto told the BBC in 1963. On his journey to their initial accommodation, he said, "I steady coughed without stopping."
Adapting to the nine-to-five work pattern also proved tricky for the community of farmers and fishermen. "Here, when you go to work in the morning, you've got one job. You've got to look forward all the whole week of getting up at the same time, going to the same place, doing the same work every day," said Joey's father Gerald, who was used to a more varied life determined by natural rhythms.
Similarly, financial pressures placed new demands on the islanders, as Swain explained. "In England, you need money for your living. But on Tristan, we don't. If we haven't got no money, well, we just go without it. It don't bother us at all… if I've got no money, I still can go out and get my own potatoes. I can still go and get my own fish."
She didn't hold back on expressing her views on British life. "We don't like the weather... There's too much sickness and we don't like the place at all."
• The tiny island seized by Britain to foil the USSR
• The greatest sailing rescue ever made
• Queen Elizabeth II's secret night out on VE Day
Despite having a single policeman on the island, who wore a British uniform, Tristan had almost no crime. The community was shocked by an incident in England when one member was attacked and hurt by two youths, who took his most valued possession, a gold watch, and smashed it.
But there were some elements of British life that were appreciated by the Tristanians, particularly the younger ones, who described a love of Italian suits and record players. "Country and western music is our favourite, by Johnny Cash and Ernest Tubb," said one teenager, who also enjoyed the social dances. "Since I come here, I've been doing the twist and the locomotion, all that lot. We've forgotten how to do the waltz. But I like to twist myself."
Despite that, most of the islanders were keen to return home. In 1962, the British government sent a survey party to study conditions on Tristan. While the volcano was still smoking, the geologists judged that it was now dormant.
Surprisingly little damage had been done to the village of Edinburgh. The lava had turned at the last moment and flowed into the sea, something that the islanders considered to be an act of God. Some of the thatched roofs were burnt, but the cottages were mostly intact. Yet in their absence, houses had been ransacked and some livestock stolen by passing sailors.
Many animals were still alive, however, with the chickens multiplying in number. Though the dogs had run wild and slaughtered the sheep, the cattle had kept themselves well-fed on the lush island grass, and there were new calves. Lava had covered the beaches, but return was possible.
The British authorities held a secret ballot in the community hall at the islanders' RAF camp. All Tristanians over the age of 21 voted, and the result was an almost unanimous vote to return, 148 to five in favour. After an advance party went back to plant seeds for the following year's potato crop, most of the islanders arrived at Tristan da Cunha in November 1963.
When asked what she was most looking forward to on the island when she returned, Swain told the BBC: "A free life. We can get our own fish and everything of our own back there without money."
Elaine Repetto, who was born on the island but chose to leave in 1984, told the BBC in 1998 why it held such a pull. "We are strongly independent and used to battling with the elements in order to survive… We have to rely upon each other in a way you would find in few other places."
She described the impact of the events in 1961. "Today, the volcano is still a smoking reminder of the events which shaped our view of ourselves and our contact with the outside world."

articles.title_orig: UCSF promises world-class care — but our patients aren’t getting it
articles.title_zh: UCSF promises world-class care — but our patients aren’t getting it
articles.content_orig:
UCSF’s $4.3 billion Helen Diller Hospital is scheduled to open in 2030, but it wont’t fix the university’s staffing crisis, write Drs. Akshar Rambachan and Anand Habib.
Every day, we watch our patients and fellow physicians pay the price for a strained system we didn’t build and can’t fix alone.
We are doctors at UCSF. At UCSF’s flagship Parnassus Hospital, people sick enough to need a hospital room wait on gurneys in emergency-room hallways because there aren’t enough staffed hospital beds.
We see patients attached to IV antibiotics laying on beds outside ER bathrooms. Elderly patients with hip fractures and pain languish under bright lights and constant noise until, deprived of sleep, they develop delirium. Families are forced to discuss end-of-life wishes within earshot of strangers in the hallway.
These are the daily realities at what should be a world-class health-care system. It’s a patient-care crisis driven by a dysfunctional system that we, as doctors, had no hand in building — or get a say in changing.
For generations, doctors had the authority and independence to make structural staffing choices to deliver high-quality patient care. Physicians owned practices, allowing them to control their patient load and shape the staffing team.
That world is disappearing. Physicians increasingly work as employees of sprawling health systems in which decisions about staffing, workload, compensation and budgets are made further and further from the bedside.
Whatever the administrators are doing clearly isn’t working. UCSF’s emergency wait time is more than 20% higher than the national average .
When UCSF patients are finally seen, their average length of patient stay is 60% higher than the state average — which strongly correlates with negative patient outcomes .
The Parnassus ER has more than double the national average of patients who leave without seeing doctors.
As doctors, we write emails, join committees, conduct studies and share proposals shaped by our years of training, research and experience to address this crisis. Our reports, requests, complaints and proposals are treated as suggestions and all but ignored.
That is why we and physicians across the University of California system are organizing a union.
She’s a longtime Democratic officeholder, but she sounds like a Main Street conservative in her campaign for the state’s No. 2 job
Following concerns over how sensitive information is accessed, mayor’s new rules would shorten data retention, require documented searches and add oversight
Annual celebration of the US Navy is zooming back into The City for seven days of festivities and the return of the elite flight squad
UCSF’s solution to the patient care crisis is the $4.3 billion Helen Diller Hospital, scheduled to open in 2030. Let us be clear — we support the new hospital. Parnassus needs more critical inpatient and emergency rooms, and our patients deserve modern facilities.
But fancy new buildings don’t treat patients — people do. The expansion can’t be a substitute for solving the real crisis: the decreased investment in frontline staffing, resulting in chronic shortages that make it impossible to provide patients with world-class care.
We are often told that capital spending and staffing come from different budgetary “pots.” The accounting may separate capital and operating expenses, but the underlying finances are interconnected. UC’s own debt policy makes that clear: Medical centers seeking external financing must demonstrate adequate operating income, cash on hand and the ability to cover their debt payments .
In other words, financing what UCSF builds for tomorrow depends on the operating performance of the health system today — which is to say, on the people doing the work.
You cannot grow a system by hollowing out the front-line workers who make it run. Commitments to adequate staffing, sustainable workloads, and retention of the people required to operate new hospitals should not be revisited every budget cycle, revocable with every change in leadership. They should be codified and fixed to maintain continuity and quality.
To deliver on our mission to do everything in our power to get the best outcomes for our patients, doctors need a say not only in how we provide care, but also in the conditions within which that care happens.
We need mechanisms to ensure sufficient staffing at all levels, guardrails on how technology is used in patient care, and safe worksites that support healthy outcomes for our patients — not wait times that cause suffering and worsen their symptoms.
Through the UC Physicians Committee, doctors across specialties and campuses are organizing with University Professional and Technical Employees union, alongside many of the pharmacists, therapists and other professionals we already work with every day.
Together, we can codify common-sense policies so that every part of a patient’s care team is set up for success.
The Helen Diller Hospital is a promise about what UCSF intends to be in 2030. The medical professionals caring for San Franciscans today deserve a binding voice in what it is now. A union is how we get one, so that the institution we’re proud to work for can be the one that its patients were promised.
Dr. Akshar Rambachan is a hospital-medicine physician at UCSF. Dr. Anand Habib is an internal-medicine physician at UCSF.

articles.title_orig: China “tests layered approach to countering drone swarms”
articles.title_zh: China “tests layered approach to countering drone swarms”
articles.content_orig:
China’s state television CCTV News shared video footage on Sunday of the People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) counter-uncrewed aerial systems (C-UAS) units in training with laser weapons, integrated missile-gun systems and high-power microwave technology as a layered defence against hostile drones.
PLA troops conducted live-fire tactical drills involving multiple day and night scenarios, CCTV said, adding that radar was used to detect a “dense swarm of drones” at low altitude. The C-UAS units then used a combination of laser ‘dazzling’ and electromagnetic measures to disrupt the formation of the swarm. Interceptor drones were also deployed as well as anti-aircraft guns.
He Qing, a PLA serviceman quoted by CCTV, said the drills combined responses to different aerial threats with battlefield operations and the handling of unexpected situations in an unfamiliar, complex desert environment.
Image: A screenshot from CCTV via Global Times

It is updated every month and broken down into niche sub-sectors (net-capture, missiles, intercept drones, detectors etc) to give C-UAS procurement and industry personnel a unique perspective of global C-UAS technical capabilities and market positions. articles.title_orig: CIP, Grok Ventures Back One of the World’s Largest-Ever Battery Storage Systems in U.S.
articles.title_zh: CIP, Grok Ventures Back One of the World’s Largest-Ever Battery Storage Systems in U.S.
articles.content_orig:
Energy Transition / Private Equity & Venture Capital / Sustainable Finance
Kenny Fisher October 5, 2026
Industrial heat and power solution provider Antora Energy announced plans for a new Kansas- based 5.8 GWh thermal battery storage project, anticipated to become one of the largest battery storage systems in the world once completed, with backing from investors including Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners and Grok Ventures.
The new battery storage project will be based at renewable fuel producer Pratt Energy’s biorefinery in Pratt, Kansas. Alongside the new project announcement, Antora also announced an offtake agreement to supply around-the-clock energy to Pratt Energy.
Founded in 2018, California-based Antora develops thermal batteries that store low-cost electricity as heat in insulated blocks of solid carbon and deliver the stored energy around the clock as industrial heat or power.
The project’s third-party equity financing was led by Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP) as part of its credit platform investments, and included participation from Australian climate-focused investment firm Grok Ventures and University Pension Plan Ontario (UPP).
Reiner Boehning, Partner at Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners, said:
“Antora has demonstrated something rare: sound technology, compelling economic fundamentals, and a clear path to repeatable deployment at scale. That gave us the conviction to partner with Antora on this project.”
Under the new offtake agreement, Antora will supply energy from the 5.8 GWh thermal battery system to Pratt Energy beginning in 2027. The battery will store low-cost electricity as heat in solid carbon blocks and supply that heat continuously to the biorefinery. The companies said that the project will improve Pratt’s operational efficiency and product competiveness, as well as supporting the company’s efforts toward producing 100% zero-carbon-intensity (CI) ethanol.
David Bierman, co-founder and Chief Commercial Officer of Antora, said:
“Our partnership with Pratt Energy delivers it, helping meet Kansas’s rising energy demand without increasing power bills for homes or businesses. This biorefinery project is creating jobs and spurring local investment without straining the resources the community depends on.”

articles.title_orig: Why India’s missile deals in Central Asia matter to Russia and China
articles.title_zh: Why India’s missile deals in Central Asia matter to Russia and China
articles.content_orig:
By supplying Akash missile systems, New Delhi offers Central Asian nations a cheap, reliable alternative
Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh confirmed the latest sales on Thursday last week, hinting at interest from elsewhere as he called the Akash “one of our success stories”.
Developed by India’s Defence Research and Development Organisation, the Akash is a home-grown, short-range surface-to-air missile system that can hit multiple targets at once and includes built-in protection against electronic jamming.
It can hit aerial targets between 100 metres and 20km (328 feet to 12½ miles) high, with an operational range of 4.5km to 25km, according to the Defence Ministry. Each 5.87-metre (19-foot) long missile weighs roughly 710kg (1,565lbs) and use command guidance to lock onto targets.

articles.title_orig: Trump Can Win Brazil and Still Lose It to China
articles.title_zh: Trump Can Win Brazil and Still Lose It to China
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump’s Washington may be about to get the Brazil it wants, a major piece of the hemispheric puzzle falling into place for the so-called “Donroe Doctrine. "
Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the right-wing son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, took 47 percent of the valid vote on Sunday to left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s 45 percent, setting up an October 25 runoff .
Trump has not formally endorsed him , but a Bolsonaro win would give the U.S. its friendliest government in Brasília since the elder Bolsonaro’s, just as Washington tries to loosen China’s grip on strategic supply chains.
China will look on nervously, but much of its groundwork in Brazil is already laid. Those foundations will be tough to break, even with a Trump-friendly Bolsonaro government in power.
The trade data shows why. In the first eight months of this year, Brazil exported $77.1 billion in goods to China, up 15 percent year-on-year, compared to just $24.1 billion to the U.S. , down 9.7 percent. That is a ratio of more than 3-to-1.
Two-way trade with China reached $128.6 billion, against $51.4 billion with the U.S. Brazil’s soybean sales to China alone outstripped everything it sold to America. And the gap is widening. A year earlier, the ratio was 2.5-to-1.
Brazil is physically closer to the U.S. and sits in the hemisphere over which Trump is asserting American hegemony. But Brasília is, in many ways, closer to Beijing than Washington.
To be sure, a Bolsonaro victory would be a real prize for Trump. But political alignment cannot repeal economic geography.
A new president can reset Brazil’s diplomatic posture in January. He cannot, at the wave of a hand, reroute the 305 million metric tons of cargo Brazil shipped to China in those eight months.
Trade on that scale doesn’t make Brazil China’s ally, though they are partnered through the BRICS bloc. But it means Beijing’s leverage depends less on who governs Brasília than on the material reality of who buys Brazil’s harvests and processes its minerals.
For evidence, look at Bolsonaro’s coalition. Brazil’s congressional farm caucus endorsed him days before the vote, and Mato Grosso, the heart of soy country, gave him about 65 percent .
Roughly 70 percent of Brazil’s soybean exports from January through August went to China. Washington cannot replace the Chinese customer. It competes with Brazil for it.
Trump’s 2025 deal with Chinese President Xi Jinping commits Beijing to buy at least 25 million metric tons of American soybeans a year through 2028. And since July, Washington has imposed a 25 percent tariff on most Brazilian goods .
Brazil has run this experiment before. Ahead of his 2018 election, Jair Bolsonaro visited Taiwan and accused China of buying Brazil . By October 2019, he was in Beijing , courting Chinese investment.
Over his term, trade with China grew, his government resisted U.S. pressure to shut Huawei out of Brazil’s 5G network entirely, and Brazil stayed in BRICS.
Rare earths, command of which will decide the great power competition in the 21 st century, make matters worse.
The younger Bolsonaro told CPAC in Texas in March that Brazil would be “the battleground where the future of the hemisphere will be fought,” and said he discussed rare earths with Trump in the Oval Office in May.
Brazil holds the world’s second-largest reserves but produced less than 1 percent of global output last year. The chokepoint isn’t the mine, but the refinery.
And here’s the difficult truth: China and Chinese-controlled firms handled 91 percent of the world’s rare-earth processing in 2024.
Pela Ema, a mine in the state of Goiás, is Washington’s showcase. About $5 billion in U.S.-backed loans, acquisition money, and price guarantees is converging on it, and last month a U.S. company bought its owner , Serra Verde.
Yet the mine yields only a mixed carbonate, an intermediate product. Separating its heavy rare earths requires a route the U.S. has not proved at commercial scale, so some output may be stockpiled.
Meanwhile, the company’s legacy contracts with Chinese processors run until the end of this year.
All of it unfolded on Lula’s watch, not a Bolsonaro. Washington’s push for Pela Ema was built on capital and guaranteed prices. No presidential sympathy needed.
What Washington still lacks is processing. No Brazilian president can conjure that. The reality is that America will rely on China for rare earths well into the 2030s .
Trump’s own January proclamation warned that even domestic mining does not safeguard national security if the U.S. “remains dependent on a foreign country for the processing.”
Washington’s has time, and it can move quickly. It assembled most of the Pela Ema package within months, and substantial new heavy-rare-earth separation capacity outside China is a few years away , roughly one Brazilian presidential term.
A Bolsonaro government could fast-track permits, court U.S. capital for new deposits, and deliver what Fernanda Magnotta of the Inter-American Dialogue expects: “ greater screening of investments in sensitive sectors .”
Pair that with U.S. tariff relief, and by 2030 Brazil could anchor a Western rare-earth supply chain even as its soybeans keep sailing to China.
The runoff can change the U.S.-China contest in Brazil without settling it. What happens next will take shape by the end of a Bolsonaro term, assuming, as all indications suggest, he will triumph in the next round.
If China’s share of Brazil’s exports, about 31 percent so far this year , has fallen below a quarter, Pela Ema’s heavy rare earths are being separated outside China at scale, and Chinese capital is screened out of strategic assets, then Washington won Brazil outright.
But if not, Trump won the palace and lost the ports.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI’s Altman: ‘The world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology’
articles.title_zh: OpenAI’s Altman: ‘The world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology’
articles.content_orig:
➡️ If you would like to receive this information in your inbox every morning before the markets open in New York, sign up here .
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Politico that people should accept the risks of AI in order to gain its benefits. “We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency,” he told the site. The trade-off will be worth it, he argued: “I wouldn’t take a trade of saying, ‘We’ll make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams, there’s zero all the other bad things that will happen’ … Because I think people will do tremendously—orders of magnitude more—good stuff than bad stuff.”
That’s a tone shift from Altman. When he talked to Fortune’s Alyson Shontell recently , he was more cautious. A 10% risk of AI killing us all by the end of the decade is unacceptable, Altman said. He insisted that OpenAI has not, and would not, take that risk.
“We are entering a new era,” he said. “We are clearly, today, at a point on the curve with great potential and real risk.”
“We have not solved alignment,” he said, referring to efforts to create AI that’s aligned with human values. “I believe no lab has solved alignment. I get nervous when I hear rumors that people think they sufficiently solved alignment, that they can continue training and it’s okay because their model is a nice guy and isn’t going to do anything wrong.”

The White House is monitoring a “plague” outbreak from a lab in Russia's Irkutsk region, according to CNBC . The incident began on Sept. 25 when a worker at an anti-plague research institute in eastern Siberia broke a test tube containing a “pneumonic plague pathogen,” according to Axios . She developed symptoms of pneumonia and then died in hospital during the night of Oct. 1-Oct. 2.
Local authorities then imposed quarantines and placed 189 people under medical observation. No further cases have been reported.
The global fertility rate for humans has never been lower, according to a recent deep-dive into global demographics from Moody's Ratings.
“The global fertility rate has declined from 4.9 children per woman in 1950 to around 2.2 today, only slightly above the replacement rate of 2.1,” the team there said. “More than 70% of the world's population now lives in countries with fertility rates at or below replacement level.” In Singapore, the government takes the problem so seriously it has started its own dating service for public employees .
The problem is that birth-rate shrinkage is a compounding problem, Moody’s says: “A fertility rate of 1.0 produces a generation roughly half the size of the one before it. At 0.8, population decline compounds even more rapidly. These effects take decades to emerge but are difficult to reverse.”
Estimates of future fertility are constantly being revised downward, as this chart from AllianceBernstein shows, implying that the problem is getting worse, faster:
A shrinking population of workers has negative consequences for economic growth, taxes, asset growth, governments’ ability to finance their debt, and inflation, most economists would agree.
Except AB’s Inigo Fraser Jenkins. “It’s probably a controversial view, but we think that fewer babies is actually a good thing. It is too late to curtail a warming of the planet by two degrees, but declining birth rates have broader implications for reducing the wider human impact on the planet and ameliorating the ‘Anthropocene.’ We are also scathing of ethical arguments that more babies are a ‘good.’”
(He and his team promised to elaborate in a forthcoming note.)
Gold has largely disappointed investors this year. After rising to around $5,340 per troy ounce at the beginning of the year, it has since lost 21% of its value and sits at $4,197. Gold now seems to be inversely correlated with U.S. interest rates, according to HSBC’s James Steel. If bonds pay higher yields, then gold (which never pays a dividend) makes less sense.
“The financial markets appear to be anticipating more substantial rate hikes, which helps explain recent gold weakness,” he said in a note. “This has been a key factor in reversing gold’s mid-summer rally.”
“As expectations for Fed rate hikes grew, gold prices weakened.”
The U.S. delivered a historically weak jobs report on Friday, with the Bureau of Labor Statistics reporting only 29,000 new roles created in September—way below expectations—and the unemployment rate moving up one tenth of a point to 4.2%.
It’s more evidence that AI is nibbling away at the job market, according to Samuel Tombs and Oliver Allen of Pantheon Macroeconomics. Although AI is creating jobs in construction and specialty trades, those gains were offset by larger declines in sectors that are the heaviest adopters of AI, like accounting, advertising, admin, legal, travel arrangement, software, and consulting.
The amount of revenue needed by the AI sector through 2032 in order to sustain its spending, according to Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh of the Columbia Business School. That’s more than spending on energy, construction, computers, defense, or the internet, the WSJ noted .

This summer, with torrential rain threatening her outdoor wedding, a bride did the one thing left on her checklist. She hired an Etsy witch to cast a spell for clear skies. She’s not the only one, according to Fortune’s Tatiana Sataua . Her bridesmaid, Brooke Bekoff, was one of roughly eight bridesmaids, and of those she said five or six had hired Etsy witches for needs of their own.
“I remember that being like, ‘Wait a minute, this is such an interesting opportunity,’” Bekoff said. “There’s really something here culturally.” After the wedding, she built Divina, a marketplace where practitioners offer tarot readings, spell work, Reiki, astrology, and other spiritual services.
The U.S. psychic-services industry generated $2.3 billion in revenue in 2025, according to a July 2025 IBISWorld report, growing at an annualized rate of 5.5%.
As for the bride? The rain continued as she got ready. But then, in a moment Bekoff described as straight out of a movie, the clouds parted right as the bridal party headed outside. Sunlight replaced the downpour, and not a single drop fell during the ceremony until it started to pour again after it ended.

articles.title_orig: China shuts hundreds of banks as Beijing moves to shore up its financial system
articles.title_zh: China shuts hundreds of banks as Beijing moves to shore up its financial system
articles.content_orig:
China is accelerating its consolidation of smaller, mostly rural banks in a bid to shore up its financial system, amid ongoing concerns over an economic slowdown in the country.
Beijing's policy-led consolidation saw a record 670 lenders closed in 2025 — about one-quarter of banks in the country — as authorities ramped up mergers and dissolutions to create fewer, larger and better-capitalized institutions, according to Fitch Ratings analysis.
Small and rural commercial banks "remain the weakest part of the system" in China, Fitch said in a report , which flagged their "poor asset quality, low capitalization and governance shortcomings," especially in less-developed regions of the country.
The rating agency said the return on assets among rural banks fell to 0.45% in the first half, down from 0.56% in 2021. Meanwhile, non-performing loans among such lenders rose to 2.8% in the same period, ahead of the sector average of 1.5%, with greater exposure to smaller companies, property developers and local government funding vehicles.
The consolidation push is aimed at boosting oversight, curbing regulatory arbitrage and improving transparency, Fitch said, noting that stress at smaller lenders is unlikely to lead to system-wide contagion, pointing to their largely localized operations and limited interbank exposure.
The measures could "ultimately reshape competitive dynamics among smaller lenders, although their structural weaknesses may persist in the near term," the rating agency added.
The move comes amid ongoing signs of strain in the world's second-largest economy.
China's GDP grew 4.3% in the second quarter, its slowest pace since 2022 , while industrial profits came in at 4.2% annually in August, their weakest pace this year.
