Physicists smashed gold nuclei together at nearly the speed of light and found an unexpected pattern in the particles these collisions sprayed out. If confirmed, that pattern could help reveal how the hot soup of quarks and gluons that filled the universe in the first few microseconds after the Big Bang cooled and condensed into the protons and neutrons that make up ordinary matter today.
In every collision, particles are flung out sideways; how hard they are flung, on average, varies slightly from one collision to the next. Physicists expected the size of these variations to change smoothly as they adjusted the collision energy. Instead, the variations dipped, shrinking and then growing again. This dip could be a sign of a long-sought "critical point," a special set of conditions at which nuclear matter changes the way it transforms from one form to another.
The signal, detected by the STAR experiment at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) at Brookhaven National Laboratory in New York, is strong enough that it is very unlikely to be a statistical accident. However, the researchers cautioned that the dip is a tantalizing hint, not proof of the long-sought transition. They published their findings Sept. 22 in the journal Physical Review Letters .
Protons and neutrons are made of smaller particles called quarks, which are held together by the " strong force " carried by particles called gluons. When heated or squeezed enough, protons and neutrons melt into a hot soup of free quarks and gluons known as a quark-gluon plasma. It's thought that this primordial soup of particles filled the universe in the first milliseconds after the Big Bang .
Physicists want to pin down how this soup-ification happened, by measuring the so-called equation of state of nuclear matter. "For water, it tells you how pressure, temperature and density are linked, and therefore when it freezes, boils or expands," study co-author Rutik Manikandhan , a postdoctoral physics scholar at The Ohio State University, told Live Science in an email. For nuclear matter, "it is the basic rulebook for matter under the most extreme conditions in nature, such as the cores of neutron stars," Manikandhan added.
The "critical point" is a key landmark in that rulebook "For water, it is the point where the boundary between liquid and steam disappears," Manikandhan said, and theorists have long suspected that nuclear matter has a similar point. At extremely high temperatures, matter melts smoothly and gradually into quark-gluon plasma, but at higher densities, the change may become abrupt.
The critical point would mark where one kind of transition turns into the other. Some recent calculations place this point within reach of RHIC's lower-energy collisions. "But all of this is still conjectured and there is nothing concrete yet, either from the experimentalists or theorists," Manikandhan said.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
The work also matters for cosmology. "Because the matter we create in these collisions resembles the matter that filled the universe a few microseconds after the Big Bang , mapping how it behaves helps us understand how the universe evolved from a hot soup of quarks and gluons into the protons and neutrons that make up everything today," Manikandhan said.
The central part of the three-story STAR detector at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC). Scientists recently used the detector to study the conditions of the early universe, just milliseconds after the Big Bang.
To explore this territory, the researchers ran RHIC at a range of collision energies. The lower the energy, the more tightly the colliding matter was squeezed. For its lowest-energy runs, STAR used a "fixed-target" setup, in which a beam of gold nuclei strikes "a thin gold foil placed inside the detector," Manikandhan said, instead of a second, oncoming beam. This produces the densest matter RHIC can make.
Collision energies are measured in electron volts (the energy an electron gains when accelerated across 1 volt). That is a minuscule amount, so particle physicists usually work in billions of electron volts, or giga electron volts (GeV). One GeV is roughly the energy locked up in the mass of a single proton, according to Einstein's famous equation E = mc 2 . The team analyzed roughly 1 billion collisions at energies between 3 and 7.7 GeV per pair of colliding protons or neutrons. That is the bottom of RHIC's range, which reaches 200 GeV.
In each collision, the team measured how hard charged particles were flung sideways out of the fireball ‪—‬ a quantity known as transverse momentum. The researchers then looked for correlations between the particles. A correlation measures whether two things tend to change together. Here, the team checked whether pairs of particles from the same collision tended to both be flung harder than average, or both more gently. That reveals something about the fireball as a whole. If a fireball is slightly hotter, or expands more forcefully, all of its particles get an extra sideways kick together.
"Those correlations reflect how much the temperature and the flow of the fireball fluctuate," Manikandhan said.
Close to a critical point, the matter's heat capacity — the amount of energy needed to raise its temperature — is expected to shoot up. That makes the fireball's temperature harder to budge, so the correlations should weaken. "If the matter approaches a critical point or a phase change, we would expect to see those correlations change in an unusual, non-smooth way as we vary the collision energy," Manikandhan said.
That is what the team saw in the most head-on collisions. "Instead of changing smoothly with energy, the correlations show a dip," Manikandhan said. The researchers compared the data with a smooth trend anchored by earlier STAR measurements at higher energies. The dip departs from that trend with a statistical significance of 5 sigma, the standard physicists usually demand before treating a signal as real. It means that if the true trend were smooth, random scatter in the data would produce such a pronounced dip only about once in 3.5 million tries.
"A smooth trend is what you'd expect from ordinary nuclear matter, so a dip suggests something more interesting is happening at those conditions," Manikandhan said.

articles.title_orig: Israeli investigators believe FlyDubai alleged hijacker was likely lone wolf, sources say
articles.title_zh: Israeli investigators believe FlyDubai alleged hijacker was likely lone wolf, sources say
articles.content_orig:
The FlyDubai alleged attempted hijacking was likely a lone-wolf attack, an early investigation by Israel shows, according to people familiar with the matter.
The investigation is still in full swing and all avenues are still being explored, the people familiar told CBS News.
The flight Wednesday from Dubai to Tel Aviv was approaching Israel when the co-pilot allegedly stabbed the flight captain and attempted to crash the aircraft , Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, passengers on board the plane and the flight captain have said.
The captain was able to fight off the co-pilot long enough to unlock the cockpit door. A group of Israeli passengers and FlyDubai staff then overpowered the co-pilot, and two off-duty pilots who were on the flight managed to gain control of the aircraft and make an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
The co-pilot is currently in the United Arab Emirates, where he is undergoing a second round of interrogation after first being questioned by Saudi authorities when the plane made its emergency landing. Israel has sent its own representatives to the UAE to participate in the investigation.
President Trump suggested Thursday that the co-pilot may be linked to Iran, "based on what I'm hearing."
"We're working on it right now," Mr. Trump said. "They're being very open with us. I would say the answer, based on what I'm hearing, is yes. But we're working on it right now."
Netanyahu told CBS News on Wednesday that the co-pilot's motives are still unknown.
"I don't think it was a hijacking," Netanyahu told "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil, adding, "I think it looks like a suicide attempt."
Speaking to Fox News on Thursday, Netanyahu said Israel knew the co-pilot "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination," based on "personal information" gathered during ongoing questioning. He did not offer any further information on the alleged indoctrination, but added to Fox that the attacker was "suicidal," and that after he was subdued by other crew members and passengers, he shouted: "Kill me, kill me!"
The co-pilot of the flight has not yet been publicly identified, although multiple sources familiar with the investigation told CBS News on Friday that his name is Hamam al Hamami.
Al Hamami worked for a short time for Oman Air, where he entered new pilot training. Surveillance by the Omani government discovered that he was visiting radical websites, the sources said. Oman Air then transferred him to an office job.
One of the sources said the pilot resigned from his job at Oman Air after being placed on desk duty. He left the airline around 2024.
At one point, sources said, al Hamami posted a video of El Al Israeli Airlines planes in Dubai with a photo at the end of the clip showing Ayman al-Zawahiri, a well-known al Qaeda leader who was killed in a U.S. drone strike in 2022.
Al Hamami moved to Dubai, and FlyDubai hired him without vetting him with the Omani government, the sources told CBS News.
Al Hamami is an Omani citizen but was not born in Oman, the sources said. He lived most of his life outside Oman, according to the sources, who disclosed that his mother is Syrian and his father is Omani.
The Omani government has not publicly confirmed his nationality.
The sources said it is possible he had dual citizenship because that could explain how he was allowed to fly to Israel.

articles.title_orig: Pope: May we pray for the intercession of the Virgin Mary for world peace
articles.title_zh: Pope: May we pray for the intercession of the Virgin Mary for world peace
articles.content_orig:
An appeal for wars to end and for peace to be built. The Pope renewed this appeal following the recitation of the Angelus prayer he led from the window of the Apostolic Palace. As he did during his recent visit to Lourdes, France, he again urged everyone to pray the Rosary for peace and unity in the world, standing in solidarity with children who have already begun doing so through the initiative of the Aid to the Church in Need Foundation, âOne Million Children Praying the Holy Rosary.â
âI wholeheartedly thank all the boys and girls who are joining in this prayer in so many parts of the world.  Let us all follow their example, invoking the intercession of the Virgin Mary so that peoples may be freed from the scourge of war.  In particular, let us pray for the Holy Land and for the innocent victims of violence.â
The campaign began at the start of October with the Pope in the Vatican Gardens and will continue until October 7, the Feast of Our Lady of the Rosary. This allows dioceses, parishes, schools, communities, and families on different continents to choose the day that is most suitable for dedicating to this particular intention.
Pope Leo then announced that, on the occasion of the tenth anniversary of Amoris Laetitia, Pope Francisâs post-synodal apostolic exhortation, a week-long gathering will begin next Wednesday, October 7.
It will be held in his presence in the Paul VI Hall, with the heads of the Eastern Churches and the presidents of the Episcopal Conferences, to take stock of the situation of families today. The gathering will include testimonies from bishops and married couples from the five continents.
It will be an opportunity to listen to the voice of the Church at a time of profound change and to find ways to renew and strengthen the choice of marriage, which in various contexts has experienced dramatic declines over the decades. The Pontiff described it this way:
âIt will be a time of synodal discernment for identifying the steps to be taken in order to proclaim the Gospel today among families and the younger generations.  I entrust this task to your prayers and, above all, the families who, with Godâs help, are a sign of hope and an inestimable treasure for the Church and for society.â
The Pope then once again held up Saint Francis as a model, as he had done during the catechesis, on the 800th anniversary of the death of Saint Francis. He expressed his happiness at the many commemorative initiatives, particularly those held in Assisi with the participation of Italyâs highest state authorities. He also offered a special greeting:
âI also greet the amateur radio operators of Assisi and Foligno who spread Saint Francisâ message of peace.â

articles.title_orig: Pre-COP31: World leaders must show up for the Pacific through action, not just speeches
articles.title_zh: Pre-COP31: World leaders must show up for the Pacific through action, not just speeches
articles.content_orig:
As Pacific leaders, communities and civil society gather in Fiji and Tuvalu for the Pre-COP31 meetings, the expected absence of many world leaders must not become another excuse for climate inaction, Amnesty International said today.
The meetings come after an unusually hot European summer, with August 2026 becoming the joint-hottest month on record. Against the looming threat of a powerful El Niño, widespread wildfires, droughts, and floods, the new UN warning of the world rapidly breaching warming thresholds adds urgency to the need for decisive climate action.
“World leaders have spent years talking about the climate threats facing the Pacific. Now they must come to Fiji and Tuvalu, listen to Pacific communities and act. Rising seas are already eating away at people’s lands, livelihoods and cultures. Concern without action will not hold back the tide,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General.
“Those who do not show up in person cannot evade their responsibilities. Their absence will not stop the seas from rising or erase the obligations of high-emitting countries towards communities paying the highest price for a crisis they did least to cause.
“An empty seat is not the greatest failure. The greater failure is an empty promise. Pre-COP31 must turn years of rhetoric into concrete commitments and action that deliver the climate ambition the world needs at COP31 in November.”
Fiji’s Environment Minister has said that the Pacific-led summit will proceed “with or without” major world leaders .
An empty seat is not the greatest failure. The greater failure is an empty promise. Pre-COP31 must turn years of rhetoric into concrete commitments and action that deliver the climate ambition the world needs at COP31 in November.
Amnesty International has documented how climate change is already harming human rights in Tuvalu, Kiribati and other Pacific Island countries . Rising seas, extreme heat, droughts and saltwater intrusion are threatening people’s rights to water, food, health, adequate housing and a safe future. Tuvalu contributes less than 0.003% of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet it faces some of the climate crisis’ most severe consequences.
During her visit to Tuvalu in 2025, Agnès Callamard witnessed efforts by communities and the authorities to reclaim land from the advancing sea and enable people to remain in their homeland.
“To any world leader who hesitates to confront the biggest crisis of our time, I say this: come to Tuvalu. Speak to people living with rising seas and extreme heat. Witness their daily struggle to adapt, protect their rights and push back against the impacts of a climate crisis they did not cause. The reclaimed land in Tuvalu is not a tourist backdrop. It represents a country fighting for its survival,” said Agnès Callamard.
Students from the Pacific took the fight against climate change to the world’s top court, leading the International Court of Justice to issue a landmark Advisory Opinion in July 2025, which made it clear that governments have a legal obligation to protect human rights from climate change impacts.
“The Pacific should not have to plead for the world’s attention. Climate action is no longer simply a political choice. It is a legal and moral imperative,” said Agnès Callamard.
“Governments must end fossil fuel use and expansion through just transitions that leave no one behind, tax big polluters and deliver scaled up grants-based climate finance, providing climate reparations and ensuring communities on the front lines of the climate crisis have the resources and power to determine their own futures. The Pacific is sounding the alarm. If the world fails to act here, it will fail everywhere.”
Climate action is no longer simply a political choice. It is a legal and moral imperative
As President of Negotiations at COP31, Australia has a particular responsibility to stand with its Pacific neighbours and secure an ambitious, human rights-centred outcome. Australia cannot credibly claim climate leadership while continuing to support fossil fuel expansion that deepens the harms facing Pacific communities.
Based on Amnesty International’s recommendations ahead of COP31 , Australia and other governments must use pre-COP31 to advance three priorities:
“Pacific leadership has helped keep the fight for 1.5°C alive, but Pacific communities cannot carry the burden of global climate leadership alone,” said Agnès Callamard. “Australia must use its presiding role to turn Pacific demands into COP31 outcomes, starting with stopping the crisis at source through a just transition away from fossil fuels.”
Governments cannot deliver climate justice while excluding affected communities or silencing those who challenge harmful projects. Across the world, Indigenous Peoples, environmental human rights defenders and communities on the front lines of the climate crisis are resisting fossil fuel expansion and fighting for fairer, more sustainable futures. Yet many face harassment, surveillance, criminalization, violence and restrictions on peaceful protest.
Australia’s treatment of peaceful climate activists will be an important test of its climate leadership. There are also concerns about restrictions on freedom of expression, association and peaceful assembly in Fiji.
Ahead of COP31, Amnesty International is launching a global campaign “ Protecting our Future: Environmental Human Rights Defenders Powering Just Transitions ” spotlighting environmental human rights defenders and the alternatives they are fighting for around the world. This includes the First Nations people in Australia , who are challenging offshore oil and gas exploration affecting their lands and waters.
The campaign will show what resistance, dignity and a people-powered just transition can look like when communities refuse to see their lands, waters and futures sacrificed for fossil fuel profits.
Australia and Fiji must ensure that civil society, Indigenous Peoples, affected communities and environmental defenders can participate, speak out and protest peacefully without discrimination, intimidation or reprisals.
“Environmental defenders are protecting our shared future. Governments must listen to them, protect them and ensure they have a meaningful say in climate decisions,” said Agnès Callamard.
“COP31 must deliver more than promises. Anything less would betray our shared responsibility to uphold human rights and secure climate justice.”
Environmental defenders are protecting our shared future. Governments must listen to them, protect them and ensure they have a meaningful say in climate decisions
The Pacific-led pre-COP31 meetings will take place in Nadi, Fiji, and Tuvalu from 5 to 8 October 2026. COP31 will take place in Antalya, Türkiye, from 9 to 20 November 2026.

articles.title_orig: Pennsylvania health officials brace themselves as measles outbreak expected to spread
articles.title_zh: Pennsylvania health officials brace themselves as measles outbreak expected to spread
articles.content_orig:
Most counties don’t have their own health agencies, and some specific population groups have low vaccination rates
Pennsylvania is bracing for a wave of measles cases, with some public health officials concerned that it’s “only a matter of time” until the disease spreads beyond the outbreak’s epicenter.
Last week the state reported its fifth measles-associated death amid 943 confirmed cases across 39 counties. The outbreak comes amid concerns that public health in the US has been hit by increasing vaccine skepticism, especially due to the power and influence of controversial health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr .
Contributing to the challenge is that Pennsylvania is one of the few US states where its counties mostly lack their own health department, with only seven of its 67 counties having their own.
Lancaster county, which doesn’t have its own health department, has seen the highest amount of cases, at 381, believed to be mostly among the Amish or similar religious groups who have historically low rates of measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine uptake. Health officials, doctors and other members of the community in the county are now attempting to establish its own health department to better tackle the outbreak.
Jeanne Franklin , the director of Chester county’s health department, said that her county, which has the third highest number of cases, at 83, is preparing for an influx of cases from neighboring Lancaster.
“We have a very long border with Lancaster county, and these types of disease don’t care about borders,” Franklin said. “It’s going to keep going and find a person who isn’t vaccinated. We’re operating with the assumption that the disease may jump and spread to non-Plain [Amish] community members. Our goal is to prevent that, but we assume that it may happen.”
She added that although many Amish people have not been vaccinated, it’s not because they are anti-vaxxers, but rather because “they were either unaware of it or they don’t seek out healthcare as frequently as other residents”.
She added: “But they’re willing to have the conversation and make a decision on what’s happening today. They’re not making decisions based on the myths out there, but because their neighbors are impacted.”
Amid active surveillance of measles cases, contact tracing and setting up community vaccination centers, the county is also working to dispel misinformation some of its residents have regarding the safety of the vaccine.
“We have people in key positions saying it isn’t an outbreak, it isn’t a problem. We have people who approach our nurses and say that they were told the vaccine will make them sterile, or that there’s a microchip within it,” Franklin said.
But for Franklin, the fact that Chester county is one of the few counties to have its own health department is a clear advantage in the race to stop the spread of the disease.
“By having our own health department [it] means that we already have the infrastructure in place, and we prepare for these things all year round,” Franklin said. “With the number of counties [the state has] to provide support to, they can’t possibly know all the key partners in a geographical area.”
She added: “The state has a finite set of employees, while I can pull my employees away from their normal jobs and say we need help with this. We live here, we know it, and we’re working with the communities and the organizations who know us. I think every county needs a health department, but we’re just not set up that way in Pennsylvania while other states are.”
Dr Richard Lorraine, the medical director of Montgomery county’s office of public health, said that it is a “matter of time” before the third most populous county in Pennsylvania will begin to see measles cases.
“We recognize that essentially it’s all around us, and so a big focus for the county is immunization,” Lorraine said. “It’s the best preventative measure and where the county is focusing its efforts on.”
after newsletter promotion
Working closely with community organizers, Lorraine said the county was making sure that every resident was able to be vaccinated regardless of their insurance status.
“Because we are a public health agency, our mandate is to provide for members of our population for the most part who are underinsured, and there’s a very high percentage who aren’t insured,” Lorraine said. “And through our partnership with pharmacies we’re able to open these clinics for everyone. So whether you have insurance or if you don’t, we can work it out so that someone is able to administer a vaccine.”
Lora Werner, the director of the Delaware county health department, said that her agency is facing several challenges in protecting residents from the virus.
Among them was the collapse of Crozer Health, Delaware county’s largest healthcare system, due to bankruptcy last year.
“They were a huge provider of pediatric care,” Werner said. “And although we do have a high vaccination rate across Delaware county, there are pockets where they aren’t as good.”
For Werner, the newly established local health department has been a gamechanger for promoting public health initiatives in the county.
“We are the newest health department on the block, and we’re so passionate about the fact that we’re now here and can serve our residents,” Werner said. “We’re deeply integrated into the social networks.”
She added: “Creating a new department was very challenging, and we’re a very odd state in this regard,” Werner said. “If you want to have one you need to have a referendum to establish one. But it’s not required, so we have a mishmash of the counties that have taken that step and those that have not.”
The Guardian has approached the Pennsylvania health department for comment.

articles.title_orig: Is a stock market correction coming? Most Americans think so
articles.title_zh: Is a stock market correction coming? Most Americans think so
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
This year has been a challenging one for Wall Street, but that hasn't seemed to slow the market down.
Despite oil price shocks, surging bond yields, and AI safety concerns, the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) has surged by more than 21% over the past six months. The tech-focused Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX: ^IXIC) has fared even better, up by nearly 30%.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
However, the question is not whether a bear market is coming, but when . Stock prices can't keep climbing forever, and at some point, the market is bound to take a turn for the worse. Preparing for that downturn, though, is simpler than you might think.
Right now is perhaps the most nerve-wracking part of the market's cycle. Stocks are still at record highs, but with so many headwinds challenging the market, it feels like we're waiting for the other shoe to drop.
Nearly 50% of investors believe stock prices will fall in the next six months, according to the latest weekly survey from the American Association of Individual Investors. If you're one of them, it can be tempting to get out of the market now while prices are still high. However, history says it's actually more lucrative to stay the course.
The market often behaves unpredictably in the near term, and it sometimes continues to surge against all odds. In 2023, for instance, strategists at Deutsche Bank warned there was a "near 100%" chance that a recession would begin in the next year, emphasizing that a soft landing would be "historically unprecedented."
Three years later, and not only has that recession not materialized yet, but the S&P 500 has surged by nearly 82%. The investors who capitalized on these returns were those who continued buying even when the future looked bleak.
To be clear, this doesn't mean that the next three years will look similar to the last three. But despite all the warning signals, the market could still have plenty of steam left before the next downturn arrives.
The smartest move investors can make right now is to buy quality stocks and prepare to hold them for at least a few years. The longer you can hold your investments, the less likely you are to lose money -- even if the market crashes right after you buy.
Say, for example, you invested in the S&P 500 in late 2007. The market was on the verge of the Great Recession, and throughout the next two years, the S&P 500 would lose more than 50% of its value. Yet over the next decade, the index surged by more than 100%.
This trend holds up throughout history, too. Between 1919 and 2025, every single one of the S&P 500's rolling 20-year periods has ended in positive total returns, according to analysis from Crestmont Research. No matter how severe the short-term volatility, the market has always managed to thrive over time.
Now, could you have earned more by only investing during the market's low points? Of course. But it's impossible to identify the market's bottom in the moment, and if you wait too long, you risk missing out on the valuable recovery period.
While it's certain that another downturn will eventually arrive, no one can say exactly when. Rather than waiting for just the right moment to buy or sell, history suggests staying in the market is the more lucrative option.

articles.title_orig: In Shanghai’s ‘Science City,’ China’s ascendant biotechs make their pitch to the world
articles.title_zh: In Shanghai’s ‘Science City,’ China’s ascendant biotechs make their pitch to the world
articles.content_orig:
This story is republished from STAT , the health and medicine news site that’s a partner to the Globe. Sign up for STAT’s free Morning Rounds newsletter here .
SHANGHAI — The biotech executives appeared triumphant.
It was a balmy, overcast Sunday here in the glimmer-and-glass “Science City” district, and the four leaders were on stage at the ballroom level of the five-star Hilton, joking about how much faster, cheaper, and more efficient drug development was here in China than anywhere else — certainly than the United States. (And God help Europe.)
Zhui Chen, cofounder of the now $6 billion Shanghai-based biotech Abbisko, recalled running a trial on a drug licensed to the German pharma Merck KGaA. Abbisko’s trial finished in 11 months, so quickly that Merck executives asked if Abbisko could train their staff.
For two years, American labs and board rooms have been riven with excitement and anxiety over the vertiginous rise of Chinese biotech. Almost overnight, it seemed, a half-century of American dominance in life sciences had evaporated. Big Pharma executives in New Jersey and New York scrambled to license drugs from Chinese companies few American scientists had ever heard of, hoping to find the next blockbuster to fill their balance sheet. Founders and investors in South San Francisco and Kendall Square watched their companies get passed over — or fold altogether — and wondered if they had a future.
To plant its own flag, Jefferies, the New York investment bank, convened its first Shanghai-based conference. The rationale was simple. The largest US life science conference is J.P. Morgan’s San Francisco summit. The largest European conference is held by Jefferies in London. China is still up for grabs.
On the main stage, panelists debated artificial intelligence, obesity, geopolitical tensions, American innovation versus Chinese execution, and the best way to commercialize a drug. Many pleaded for collaboration, not competition.
Executives walked through their pipelines in English, flashing antibody drugs in full Revlon counter variety. Local representatives from hulking multinationals like GSK, Merck, and Sanofi roamed the halls, scouting potential prospects. A contingent from SK Biopharmaceuticals, the Korean pharma, filled an elevator.
Even longtime veterans of the drug industry here struggled to make sense of what they’re seeing.
“It’s really blowing like everyone’s mind, right?” said Betty Huang, who helps spearhead Chinese business development for the German pharma Bayer.
Behind closed doors, a new wave of deals were coming to the fore. Cui Cui, Jefferies’s head of health care research for Asia, told local media that investors had traveled from Brazil and South America. The Shanghai conference was appended to a broader Asia tour, and Cui said she had met with representatives from a Texas teachers’ pension fund in Korea who “are very interested in China” — though they can’t invest for “various reasons.”
Venrock and other US VC firms had staff on site, talking trades and scoping out local operations. One US-based investor was trying to decide if they needed to hire someone in the region full time. Michael Garrow, chief investment officer of HS Group, a Hong-Kong based investment firm that backs specialized hedge funds, was meeting with portfolio managers to see if it was time to reinvest. Could he find “the RTW or RA Capital of Asia?” he said, naming prominent US health care funds.
A decade ago, health care-focused firms had popped up and flamed out in Asia. But now, there seemed to be “real innovation,” he said.
It was a well-timed summit. Two days before kickoff, the Chinese government issued its latest five-year-plan for biotech. By 2030, it wrote, Chinese drug developers should have at least five blockbuster drugs. One fourth of all first-in-class drugs should come out of China.
Bold, to say the least. Today, Chinese drugmakers have one or two blockbusters.
It’s hard, though, to see the latest frenzy of dealmaking and see anything but a diagonal line pointing up. The numbers vary, depending on which bank, consulting firm, or analyst you trust. But Chinese-designed drugs now make up about a third of the world’s pipeline and draw more than half of all licensing or collaboration deals, as measured by total dollar value.
Morgan Stanley seems to be a believer, projecting Chinese-designed drugs will account for 35 percent of all Food and Drug Administration approvals by 2040, compared to 5 percent today. So is Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla, who warned an Atlantic Council audience recently that the gravity had already shifted.
“I don’t want to lose the superiority of the US biopharma to the Chinese, which I see that happening in five years,” he said. “I don’t want that to happen. But we are putting 80 percent of our energy to think how to slow them down rather than 80 percent of our energy to see how we can become better than them.”
The Chinese government has been trying to steward biotech here for years, with mixed success. In the 2000s, large pharmas like GSK and Novartis set up R&D centers here, but most of them ultimately pulled back, with little to show for the lucre spent.
Most observers point to 2015 as the pivotal moment. The government started speeding review of new trials and approvals and brought its clinical trial system in line with international standards. In 2018, the Hong Kong stock exchange allowed unprofitable companies to go public, thus boosting biotech fundraising and VC returns.
Meanwhile, Chinese contract research organizations and manufacturing companies, like Wuxi AppTec, grew remarkably efficient, in part by working with American companies. Local scientists learned drug development inside these CROs, or the local divisions of Big Pharma. Or they trained abroad and came home.
American companies still work with the CROs, which are tightly woven into the ecosystem here. “A Chinese scientist who is using a CRO can just ride a bike and supervise them on how to do the science,” said one prominent Chinese biotech venture capitalist. “Unlike sitting in Boston, where you send an email and they respond a day later.”
Meanwhile, companies can enroll patients faster because large hospitals attract thousands of patients for care.
The result is companies that can engineer molecules every which way with ruthless efficiency and put them into early development on the cheap. After mastering generics, companies moved on to me-too-drugs, then me-better, and now are competing with US companies to develop more novel compounds.
Today, the old GSK building is occupied by Abbisko, beside other local pharma companies in an office park that features a KFC and Starbucks. Their scientists, typically making around 50 percent of what a US scientist would make, contribute to a system that is about 50 percent to 70 percent faster than the rest of the world in developing trial-ready molecules and then two to five times faster at recruiting patients for late-stage trials, per McKinsey estimates .
Ying Huang, who steered the Chinese-founded startup Legend Biotech as it beat out US competitors to develop a powerful cancer cell therapy Carvykti, sat on the same panel as Chen, the Abbisko cofounder. He said his distressed Boston colleagues complain that office and lab space in Kendall Square is vacant and they can’t get funding.
“We all know that this is the competition,” said Huang, who lives in New Jersey and now runs a startup licensing molecules out of China. “Whoever is more innovative, whoever is more efficient, will get investment.”
For all the fanfare, few thought — or at least would say — that the US biotech industry would wither away. Kendall Square would survive, assured Eric Liu, managing director of Banyan BioInnovations, a new China-focused offshoot of the life sciences investment bank Locust Walk.

articles.title_orig: I place the world's top software engineers and interviewed over 10,000 job seekers. The difference on paper and in person is wider than ever
articles.title_zh: I place the world's top software engineers and interviewed over 10,000 job seekers. The difference on paper and in person is wider than ever
articles.content_orig:
Paddy Lambros is founder and CEO of AI recruiter Dex.
Go to LinkedIn on any given day and you can read horror stories of hiring managers receiving thousands of AI-generated CVs, or applicants applying unsuccessfully for thousands of roles.
But while hiring is an undoubtedly dysfunctional process (one we are trying to fix, by the way) the main reasons that people don’t get hired existed long before AI.
Before I built an AI recruitment startup for software engineers, I worked in actual recruitment, finding the best tech talent for companies like Microsoft , Accenture , Deloitte.
I’ve interviewed thousands of applicants, and it is fair to say I’ve seen a few interview train-wrecks. But my main takeaway is that the reasons people don’t get hired are relatively simple – and avoidable – and that, as an applicant, you really have to do very little to stand out.
You can’t win on the strength of your CV, but you can lose.
If you send out a document that looks terrible, is full of spelling mistakes or doesn’t make sense, then you are sending a pretty negative signal of what you think good work looks like.
The main reason CVs fail is because they talk guff: “I conceptualised the Q3 planning process” or some such nonsense.
You need to be concrete: ‘I helped build X. I helped the company sell more Y’ or ‘This is what I did, and this is how it happened.’
You would not believe how many people fail at this point.
I’ve put out job specs for entry level roles and – at the bottom – given my email and asked candidates to reach out and tell me why they want the job. 90% of people don’t.
I remember putting out an advert for a very junior role with a box that said: ‘Tell me why you’d be great fit for this job’ and most people didn’t fill it in. It is baffling.
I always respond to people who write something interesting in that box. You need to act like you really want the job.
And if you are asked to do an exercise as part of the application process, then do it.
I’ve heard people say that they won’t work for free or are worried that the company will not hire them and steal their work, but honestly, it is a delusion.
If the company is interviewing people, then they really want to hire someone and they’re trying to work out if you could be that person.
If you really think you can produce better work in a couple of hours than the team working on it full time, then you’re either the best in the world or they are rubbish, in either case you probably shouldn’t be interviewing there.
You often see people claiming that they have applied for 1,000 jobs and got no responses: Well, nobody is qualified for 1,000 jobs. You are wasting your time.
Take that time and spend it researching five jobs and really putting the effort in.
I get that people are playing the volume game but most jobs that people are applying for they are either not qualified for – or aren’t right for them. But if they’d actually gone through the job spec, they’d realise that.
Hiring is a high-stakes game: 50% of new highs fail or quit in 18 months and only one in five new hires is considered a success after 12 months.
Consider the impact that has on a business: not only all the work – and cost – involved with finding the right candidate and hiring them, but the impact that an unsuccessful hire has on the rest of the team. This is all the more acute in startups, which tend to have very small teams.
So, when you walk into that job interview feeling nervous, remember that the person interviewing you may be just as nervous. They may have been through this a few dozen times already. They may have one or two bad hires behind them.
And remember it is a two-way street. The interviewer wants to get to know you, but you need to get a handle on this company too. Do you want to spend 80% of your waking hours here?
Honestly, one of the main reasons people fail an interview is because they are unable to answer this question.
I get that they are worried it will make them look bad, but it will make you look much worse if you can’t answer it.
It is inconceivable that your interviewer would never have made a mistake, so be honest, open up, and don’t turn this into an opportunity to blow your own trumpet.
There is nothing more valuable in hiring than a personal recommendation or a referral.
It should be a reminder that growing and maintaining your professional network is a key part of your career. You need to be a person others would vouch for.
And people don’t vouch for people just because they like them, they vouch for people who do a good job. They want to know that when they say: ‘You should hire this person’ and they do, you turn out really well.

articles.title_orig: Tens of thousands protest against Spain's housing crisis following eviction of 87-year-old woman
articles.title_zh: Tens of thousands protest against Spain's housing crisis following eviction of 87-year-old woman
articles.content_orig:
Demonstrators take to the streets of Madrid ⁠and other Spanish cities ⁠after ​new legislation fails to pass
Tens of thousands of people have taken to the streets of Madrid ⁠and other Spanish cities as they step up demands for action to tackle ⁠a mounting housing crisis ⁠after ​government measures were struck down by the opposition.
Demonstrators on Saturday waved posters calling for a general strike ⁠after the measures drawn up to address mass anger over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman in ⁠Madrid, and other housing issues, were rejected in parliament on ​Friday.
Authorities said 70,000 people were protesting. Organisers put the figure at 500,000.
“It’s a shame,” Nando ‌de Anguulo, 26, ‌who joined the protest in Madrid, told Reuters. “It only proves that it ‌is us, the people, who have to adapt to the political parties, and not the politicians to what the people want, and this can’t go on like that.”
Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, may call a snap election for November after the ‌legislation failed to pass, Spanish media reported on Friday, and would be watching the strength of Saturday’s ​protests before making a decision.
The demonstrations have dominated the national conversation, breathing new life into Sánchez’s beleaguered government and shifting attention away from the lingering impact of recent events in Ceuta .
Protests on Saturday were peaceful in 50 Spanish cities. In the south-eastern city of Valencia, demonstrators clashed with police who fired rubber bullets and teargas ⁠to break up the protests.
About 30 people managed to get inside ​the City ​of Arts and Sciences, a ​landmark cultural building in the city, before they were ​ousted by ‌police.
One protester in Madrid, Marcos Sainz, a librarian, 26, said he used to rent a two-bedroom apartment with friends for a monthly rent of 900 euros ($1,000) but that a one-bedroom flat often now cost 1,000 euros – or half the median monthly salary in the capital.
He told AFP he would protest rental spikes “until someone dares to regulate it all, as (otherwise) we’ll all have to leave Madrid and that would be a shame as I am from Madrid”.
Javier, 31, a solar panel installer, said: “We are demanding a fundamental right: decent housing, stability and conditions allowing us to construct a decent life project.” He added: “I spend half of my salary on a tiny room.”
“What we are feeling in the streets is a new energy that we haven’t seen in a long time, an energy that is showing that eight days of people power can achieve more than eight years of progressive government,” Valeria Racu, one of the spokespeople of the Tenants’ Union organising the protest, said in a statement.
“Now begins real politics – politics which has always belonged to the people and which will return once and for all to the streets,” she said.
after newsletter promotion
Late on Saturday groups of far-right protesters, some of them performing Nazi salutes, tried to get to the camp in Madrid but were blocked by police.
One video posted on the website of Spanish daily El País showed police chasing some members of the group through the streets and the newspaper also reported that officers had made three arrests.
On Friday, Sánchez’s Socialist-led coalition put forward two decrees that included a range of measures aimed at improving access to housing, from a ban on evictions until 2030 to the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room.
Despite the anger of the protesters outside parliament, the conservative People’s party, the far-right Vox and the Catalan pro-independence party Junts voted against both decrees.
The People’s party said it had voted in line with its belief that building, rather than regulating, was the best way to address the crisis. “Housing doesn’t become more affordable through decrees; it becomes more affordable by building ​more homes,” said the lawmaker Juan Bravo.
News of the package’s rejection was met with boos and cries of “shame” outside. “Your profits, our misery,” the protesters chanted.
The long-simmering anger at soaring housing costs boiled over late last month, when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who uses a wheelchair, was evicted from the home she had lived in for 70 years . The octogenarian said she was unable to afford the 230% rent hike demanded by the investment fund that bought her apartment.
Reuters and AFP contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: China's railway passenger trips hit record single-day high
articles.title_zh: China's railway passenger trips hit record single-day high
articles.content_orig:
Passengers line up at the boarding gates at Shenzhen North Railway Station in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, October 1, 2026. /VCG
China's railway network handled 25.204 million passenger trips on October 1, the first day of the week-long National Day holiday, setting a new single-day record, China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. (China Railway) said Friday.
On October 2, the railway network is expected to handle 20.39 million passenger trips, with 1,462 additional trains scheduled to meet the high demand, the company said.
Passenger ticket pre-sales show that the most popular departure cities on Friday include Beijing, Guangzhou, Shanghai, Chengdu, Shenzhen, Hangzhou, Wuhan, Xi'an, Zhengzhou and Nanjing, while popular arrival cities include Beijing, Guangzhou, Chengdu, Hangzhou, Shanghai, Wuhan, Xi'an, Zhengzhou, Nanjing and Changsha.
Routes such as Xi'an-Chengdu round trips, as well as those from Beijing to Shenyang, Zhengzhou and Qingdao are among the busiest.
Railway authorities across the country have strengthened transport organization and implemented measures to ensure safe, convenient and comfortable travel.
China Railway Taiyuan Group has coordinated with local transport departments and scenic spots to add shuttle buses linking Datong South Station with the Yungang Grottoes, a UNESCO World Heritage site featuring more than 50,000 Buddhist stone sculptures, and the Hengshan Mountain scenic area in north China's Shanxi Province.
China Railway Hohhot Group has added 11 multiple-unit trains to the Baotou-Wuhai section of the Baotou-Yinchuan high-speed railway.
China Railway Wuhan Group, tapping the newly opened Yichang-Xingshan high-speed railway, has launched a promotion campaign with local governments in Yichang and Xingshan, offering passengers exclusive discounts at scenic spots, hotels and homestays when they present their train tickets.
China Railway expects some 284 million passenger trips during the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holiday period, which runs from September 23 to October 8.

articles.title_orig: Government forces seize capital of Ethiopia's Tigray region from rebels
articles.title_zh: Government forces seize capital of Ethiopia's Tigray region from rebels
articles.content_orig:
By Deborah Castellano Lubov
"Above all, the Ethiopian Catholic Church earnestly calls upon all parties to open their hearts to forgiveness and reconciliation by renewing the spirit of brotherhood and sisterhood among us, so that our nation may experience a just, lasting, and authentic peace."
This was the appeal emphasized by the Catholic Bishops of Ethiopia in a letter issued by the Catholic Bishopsâ Conference of Ethiopia (CBCE) on Thursday.
The message began by stressing that the Ethiopian Catholic Church grieves deeply over the armed conflict currently present in Tigray, Afar, Amhara, Oromia, and other regions of the country.
"Rather than resolving differences," the Bishops said, "war serves only to deepen divisions and multiplies suffering. It claims a tragic toll on precious human lives, inflicts grave devastation upon communities and property, and sows seeds of hatred, resentment, and vengeance that may endure for generations."
The African Bishops echoed Pope Leo's appeal for peace at his Wednesday General Audience, after his return from his Apostolic Journey to France, where he said he was following with deep concern the situation in Tigray and in the neighboring regions of Afar and Amhara, where hostilities have once again broken out.
"I extend," the Holy Father said, "my heartfelt plea to all parties to choose the path of dialogue. Armed conflict never solves problems but only worsens them, leaving in its wake a trail of death, destruction, and resentment. Only honest engagement can lay the foundations for lasting peace."
In continuity with the Holy Father's exhortation, the nation's Catholic Bishops appealed in their statement "to regard the life of others as we regard our own life and the suffering of others as our own suffering, because the peace of our beloved nation, Ethiopia, is a responsibility shared by all of us."
"It is our heartfelt prayer," they wrote, "that all disputes may be settled through genuine dialogue and that all forms of conflict may cease."
In a special way, they recalled the "painful" reality that whenever violence erupts, the greatest suffering falls upon the most vulnerable, particularly innocent people, children, women, the elderly, and the sick.
"We continue to raise our voice," the bishops said, "so that this may not happen and to implore the Lord to protect every human life. We therefore affirm that a peace rooted in truth, justice, forgiveness, and reconciliation can bring healing to our nation and serve the welfare of all our peoples. Such a peace reflects the values of the Gospel, advances the common good, upholds the sacred dignity of the human person, and corresponds to the will of God for His people."
The Bishops urged all Catholic faithful and all people of good will to persevere in prayer and fasting, imploring Almighty God to bestow upon their nation the blessings of reconciliation, unity, and lasting peace.

articles.title_orig: ‘Adua’ Collaboration Is Born From a Flower Between Worlds
articles.title_zh: ‘Adua’ Collaboration Is Born From a Flower Between Worlds
articles.content_orig:
Artwork by Karen Paulina Biswell & Maria Amilbia Siagama Siagama
Words by Karen Paulina Biswell
My collaboration with María Amilbia Siagama Siagama began 15 years ago, when I met her daughter in the streets of Bogotá, and continued into the mountains of Risaralda. It has been driven by curiosity, the desire to know one another, and learning to accept the opacity and misunderstandings that run through our relationship.
Our joint project, ADUA , takes its title from the Embera word for “I don’t know”—an embrace of uncertainty that offers a form of kinship that doesn’t erase difference, but learns to live with and through it. It also makes space for what does not need to be translated or explained.
My conversations with María Amilbia led me to the Benakúa ceremony, where men of knowledge drink a preparation made from the Brugmansia flower and travel to the underworld. For the Emberá, getting drunk and dreaming are intertwined: seeing and dreaming can become the same experience. What interested me was this idea of “knowing through forgetting.” What would it mean to forget the ways we had learned to see Indigenous communities? For me, it meant forgetting myself, opening myself to others, and allowing dreaming to become a way of seeing.
At the heart of ADUA is the Brugmansia, or iguaka, a sacred plant understood by the Emberá Chamí as a spiritual master and companion species. Its downward-facing flowers are associated with the world beneath us, a realm of knowledge and wisdom. In the Benakúa ceremony, the journey to this underworld can bring back guidance for tending the territory.
In these images, the Brugmansia becomes a kind of satellite between worlds—between seeing and dreaming, knowing and forgetting, memory and belief. It is through the flower that ADUA asks how we might encounter one another without needing to make everything fully known.

articles.title_orig: Florida weighs ditching property taxes and sticking Canadians with the bill
articles.title_zh: Florida weighs ditching property taxes and sticking Canadians with the bill
articles.content_orig:
Florida voters are weighing whether to scrap residential property taxes, and the state's governor has a solution to that potentially huge revenue loss: tax Canadians more.
Canadians who own property in Florida describe the threats to shake them down for more money as just the latest insult in a series of them since U.S. President Donald Trump returned to power last year with a decidedly anti-Canada agenda.
Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis has railed against property taxes, which fund local governments and the services they provide — law enforcement, fire, EMS, disaster preparation and mosquito control, among many others — equating them to a form of modern-day feudalism where homeowners must "pony up money to the government just for the courtesy of using your own property."
To end this, DeSantis is pushing Amendment 3, a ballot measure crafted by his Republican statehouse allies that will be put to voters in the midterm election next month.
If passed, Florida "homesteaders," as permanent residents are called, will see a dramatic increase in an existing property tax exemption.
Any Floridian with a primary residence valued at $250,000 US or less — about 60 per cent of all homesteaders, according to the governor's office, although that figure has been questioned — would pay nothing, and those with a home worth more than that would pay much less than they do now. The measure also calls on the state to eliminate homesteader property taxes entirely over time.
This constitutional amendment requires a 60 per cent supermajority, and at least one recent poll suggests it will easily clear that hurdle .
State economists project such a move will cost about $12 billion US annually , forcing local and county governments that depend on these taxes to make deep cuts, find new revenue elsewhere or both.
That's where things could get more expensive for the Canadians who own an estimated $60 billion US worth of property in the Sunshine State. DeSantis has explicitly described them as a resource to tap to close expected budget gaps.
"We need to focus on our Florida residents. And focus on, in this case, Florida homeowners, particularly our homesteaded homeowners, and we need to focus the relief there," DeSantis said at a news conference last year defending his call for lower property taxes instead of a sales tax cut.
"I want Canadian tourists and Brazilian tourists subsidizing the state and making it so Florida residents pay less taxes. I don't want to give Canadians a tax cut."
In an interview with Fox Business in June, DeSantis said that while homesteader property tax revenue will be a fraction of what it once was if the measure passes, Canadian property owners won't see any of that relief, which could help pad local coffers.
"They tax property that is non-homestead: residential, Airbnb, Canadian snowbirds, commercial. That's a lot of money that they have," DeSantis said of local and county governments.
While reducing taxes for Floridians, the ballot measure also dictates that the assessed value of a non-homesteaded property — owned by a Canadian or another non-resident — can increase by up to five per cent a year, steadily raising the revenue local governments can collect.
"They are going to start getting more revenue from existing taxes without having to add new taxes, and they're going to end up in a very stable situation very shortly," DeSantis said.
DeSantis has routinely poked at Canada — including its perennially losing hockey teams. He initially mocked the trade war-induced travel boycott, saying he didn't think it would meaningfully materialize, only to see his state tourism bureau report a double-digit drop in Canadian arrivals last year.
Some Canadians who have put down seasonal roots in the state have had enough of the taunts.
Glenn McGill of Wiarton, Ont., has been wintering in North Fort Myers, Fla., a community once well populated with fellow Canadian sunseekers, for the last 15 years.
But after Trump's second win, there's been what he describes as a "stampede" of Canadians out of the park he and his wife Deb long thought of as a second home.
He says there are only four Canadians left in the sprawling retirement community, a fraction of what there once was when he first started going south.
Some snowbirds want out of Florida. A bad housing market makes it hard to leave
McGill said DeSantis's threat to lean on Canadians to make up for lost property tax revenue will only drive more of them away, including himself — he listed his home for sale.
"They're a greedy bunch of SOBs," McGill said in an interview with CBC News. "They want to drive Canadians out."
"Those who are well off really don't care, but we're not rich, we're not broke, we can do the Florida thing comfortably, but starting to pay extra taxes — that would hurt," he said.
"And this political thing with Trump, I've had enough of it."
With so many Canadians leaving or staying away, McGill says the housing market in Florida has been tough to navigate as a seller.
"The market's pretty dry," he said. "It's listed, but it hasn't sold yet."
Canadians make up the vast majority of foreign property buyers in areas along Florida's Gulf Coast.
According to Realtor.com data, Canadians represent more than 70 per cent of international demand in the Cape Coral metropolitan area, which includes McGill's community.
And with Canadian sales nowhere near pre-trade war levels , the firm says local sellers face " real pricing pressure ," with properties listed for weeks longer than the national average .
The areas of Florida that have historically attracted the most Canadian interest are projected to see the largest drop in home prices this year, according to the firm's projections.
Edie Ousley, a spokesperson for Vote No on 3, a group opposing the property tax ballot measure, anticipates more housing market shocks given a possible flood of new Canadian-owned home listings if this tax change takes effect.
"Gosh, it wouldn't surprise me if there's an exodus of Canadians — they are going to be hit significantly," Ousley said in an interview.
"Amendment 3 is a train wreck. It's a train wreck for Floridians. It's a train wreck for those who come in the winter. Those Canadian snowbirds are going to be impacted with additional taxes — this is a tax shift, it's not tax relief," she said.
Ousley said a shrinking Canadian population base alone can't replace what will be lost if homestead taxes disappear.
Many municipalities are already warning that a sudden erosion in their tax base will decimate public services, most notably law enforcement and 911 response times.
"Everyone is going to lose with cuts," she said.
John May of Ottawa offloaded his Key West, Fla., condo after getting sick of hearing people he thought were friends parrot Trump's harsh rhetoric about Canada.
He said he felt like he was swimming in "a sea of stupidity," with falsehoods about his country commonplace.
"Trump would say something stupid, Governor Trudeau, 51st state and all that, and they'd stand there and laugh and I'd say to myself, 'Well, I just lost all respect for you,'" May said in an interview.
"And then you start avoiding people because you know what the conversation is going to be. If you try and have a logical discussion with somebody who's a Trumper, just forget about it."
Jo-Ann Rowe, a Canadian who was wintering in Fort Lauderdale for years with no issue before Trump's return, had the same experience.
"The 51st state thing, my American friends all thought that was quite funny. And I really don't," she said.
She left Florida for a rental property in Puerto Vallarta, Mexico. "I found it totally disrespectful. And I just couldn't do it anymore, this was my little part to do," she said.
Lilly White of Almonte, Ont., spent the last 25 years going to Tarpon Springs, Fla., near Tampa and then Flagler Beach on the other side of the state to escape Canadian winters.
White describes her time there in glowing terms, but said things changed dramatically i

articles.title_orig: Report says heat, fires left a third of the world living with 'extremely poor' air quality
articles.title_zh: Report says heat, fires left a third of the world living with 'extremely poor' air quality
articles.content_orig:
A European Union analysis released on Sept. 30 suggests that adding heat waves and wildfire smoke to existing air pollution has exposed about a third of the world's population to what it classified as "extremely poor" air quality.
Malay Mail reported that the European Union's Copernicus Climate Atmosphere Monitoring Service said 34% of people worldwide faced what it labeled "extremely poor" air quality from Jan. 1 through Sept. 15.
Another 17% of the global population fell into the "very poor" category, and only 5% reached what it described as "good" ozone levels.
Asia was hit the hardest, with 53% of the region's population in the "extremely poor" category and another 22% in "very poor" ozone conditions.
Those exposure categories were measured against World Health Organization guidance that caps eight-hour ozone exposure at 100 micrograms per cubic meter.
On hot, sunny days, pollution from vehicles, industry, and wildfires can react in the air to create ground-level ozone, a pollutant that can turn already polluted conditions into a major health risk.
Health effects can include damaged lung tissue, trouble breathing, and asthma attacks.
According to the analysis, record heatwaves and wildfires in Europe and North America helped drive the increase, with smoke spreading far beyond the burned areas.
Ozone has been especially hard to bring down, even as some other harmful pollutants have declined, because climate conditions make it easier to form. The analysis also pointed to major wildfires in Indonesia and said El Niño, which began in June, could contribute to more fires in Southeast Asia.
The Copernicus Climate Atmosphere Monitoring Service tracks pollution and wildfire activity using satellite data and computer models.
That helps explain why ozone remains a stubborn problem even after declines in some other major air pollutants over recent decades.
Dangerous air is not always local or visible. A stretch of hot, sunny weather combined with smoke or urban pollution can worsen air quality even far from a wildfire, making air-quality alerts more important during heat events.
As CAMS director Laurence Rouil said in the Atmosphere Watch report: "Air pollution does not stop at borders. It can travel thousands of kilometres, crossing continents and oceans and affecting air quality far from its source."
These stories look at the same ozone and smoke threats highlighted in this report.
• Across the U.S., blazing heat and wildfires are wiping out air quality gains .
• Across the U.S., wildfire-driven ozone is linked to premature deaths far from the flames.
• In China, scientists found that winter ozone pollution can spike even without summer heat.

articles.title_orig: World’s largest oat milk producer joins climate journalism campaign
articles.title_zh: World’s largest oat milk producer joins climate journalism campaign
articles.content_orig:
NEW YORK -- Oatly, the world's largest producer of oat milk, is sending a new message to its consumers: Most people want their governments to take action on climate change.
Splashed on the side of the Swedish company's cartons is messaging from the "89 Percent Project," a campaign launched by Covering Climate Now, a global journalism nonprofit.
Newsrooms traditionally try not to associate with organized advocacy efforts, but the unorthodox campaign has been gaining traction. Participating news organizations have amplified research that 80% to 89% of people worldwide want their governments to confront climate change.
Oatly's new cartons were first released in Sweden and have since been rolled out to other European nations, including Belgium and Germany. The cartons are expected to be on U.S. shelves by January, said Caroline Reid, senior sustainability director at Oatly.
"Companies should be taking much more responsibility, not only in reducing their own environmental footprint, but really working out how they can use their platform to drive a positive future," Reid said at an event last month during New York Climate Week.
In addition to producing stories on climate change, Covering Climate Now promotes reporting on the issue through journalism trainings, newsroom collaborations and press awards. It launched the "89 Percent Project" last year and describes it as a global collaborative journalism initiative.
The project takes its name from a 2024 study in the peer-reviewed scientific journal Nature Climate Change. Based on a survey of nearly 130,000 people across 125 countries, the study found that 89% of people want intensified political action on climate change.
Most people who want climate action don't realize they are in the "silent majority," said Mark Hertsgaard, executive director of Covering Climate Now. But that is beginning to change, as "elements of civil society all around the world pick up this 89% message and spread it themselves."
The project launched with several media partners, including The Guardian, Agence France-Presse and El País. In April, Japanese TV stations said over the next two years they would air announcements about how the majority of Japanese people want stronger climate action. In June, in a separate initiative, 136 Japanese news outlets also began spreading this messaging via social media platforms, news releases, and other forms of public communication.
Numerous polls, surveys and scientific studies in the U.S. have long found that a majority want the government to take more action on climate change, even if the issue is rarely brought up in political campaigns.
In a 2022 poll, The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that nearly two-thirds of Americans thought the federal government was not doing enough to fight climate change, which is primarily caused by the release of greenhouse gases when coal, oil and gas are burned.
That same year, a study based on responses from more than 6,000 Americans and published in the peer-reviewed scientific journal Nature Communications found that most Americans underestimate the prevalence of support for major climate change mitigation policies and climate concern. While 66% to 80% of Americans support these policies, Americans think only 37% to 43% do.
"We felt that we, and our fellow journalists, were really missing the story here," said Hertsgaard, adding he believed the industry was inadvertently "misrepresenting a big part of the climate story, which is that most people around the world want this tackled."
Oatly's milk carton campaign is subtle, especially when compared to the more well-known 1980s U.S. milk carton campaign that put photos of missing children on cartons to spread awareness about their cases.
The new cartons feature two stacked text boxes on one side of the carton.
The much smaller top box reads: "Politicians! These eleven words represent people not interested in climate action." The lower box, which takes up most of the carton's side, has an 89-word message that makes the case that most people want their governments to take climate action and that doing so could lead to political wins.
Reid, with Oatly, first read about the climate project in The Guardian. As a company selling alternatives to cow milk, she said the project "aligns with what we're trying to do. We're trying to engage people and make them want to do something different."
Every organization, political party and brand can play a bigger role in contributing to societal net zero, meaning as much carbon being absorbed as is released into the atmosphere, and driving the transition to renewable energy, Reid said.
President Donald Trump has periodically railed about climate change and policies meant to address it, including transitioning to carbon-free energy like wind and solar. During the 2025 U.N. General Assembly, Trump called climate change a "con job" and renewable energy the "Green Scam."
This narrative, which goes against years of science that has established that human-caused emissions are driving the climate to change, has pushed some organizations to take a stronger stand in rebutting the administration and go a step further to advocate for solutions.
Covering Climate Now's project straddles a tightrope between advocacy and journalism, which experts say has pros and cons.
"The economic failures of so many news outlets have led to a rise in independent journalism that operates outside the norms established by legacy media outlets," said Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation. "There is plenty of room for advocacy in journalism."
Clay Calvert, who specializes in First Amendment and freedom of expression issues at the University of Florida, said two dangers arise when journalism organizations partner with companies.
The first is that the journalism group will pull its punches and self-censor negative information about the corporate partner. The second is that the journalism organization will favorably portray its corporate partner in news coverage.
"There really needs to be a wall of separation in any newsroom between the interests of the journalism entity, including its readers and viewers, and those of its corporate partners," Calvert said. "Sometimes creating and maintaining that separation is easier said than done."
No money has changed hands between Covering Climate Now and Oatly, according to Hertsgaard, who called the company an "ally."
"As a journalist, I feel like we have to have the courage to not just report the facts, but to draw the connections," Hertsgaard said. "Now, if that amounts to advocacy, then that's an advocacy I'm comfortable with."
Information for this article was contributed by Jennifer McDermott of The Associated Press.

articles.title_orig: US Department of Justice indicts CEO for smuggling ‘AI chips’ into China
articles.title_zh: US Department of Justice indicts CEO for smuggling ‘AI chips’ into China
articles.content_orig:
A California technology entrepreneur accused of helping move more than $300 million worth of export-controlled computer servers to China is at the center of one of the largest recent U.S. cases involving advanced artificial intelligence hardware and export restrictions.
Federal authorities arrested Greg Lui, 38, on Thursday, alleging he orchestrated a scheme to send high-end computer servers containing advanced U.S.-made graphics processing units, or GPUs, to China through third countries in violation of federal export-control laws.
Lui, also known as Yiu Kong Lui, faces charges of conspiracy to violate export-control regulations, smuggling, and conspiracy to commit money laundering. If convicted on all counts, he could face up to 50 years in prison.
According to federal prosecutors, Lui owns Earthmade Computer Inc., a technology company based in the City of Industry in Los Angeles County.
Public business profiles show Earthmade was founded in 2021 and operated in areas including server procurement, technology infrastructure, and data-center services.
According to public profiles, Lui's technology career began with work in hosting and colocation services before he launched Earthmade Computer. The company marketed itself as a provider of server procurement, infrastructure, and data-center solutions, placing it in the fast-growing market for advanced computing hardware during the boom in artificial intelligence investment.
Before entering the technology sector, Lui was involved in the restaurant business. Public profiles indicate he helped launch a San Gabriel Valley restaurant specializing in Sichuan cuisine before later transitioning into technology and data-center operations.
Authorities allege Earthmade became the vehicle through which export-controlled AI hardware was purchased and routed overseas.
The Justice Department said Earthmade received more than $176 million from two Malaysia -based shipping companies between January and October 2024 as part of the alleged operation.
Newsweek has reached out to Earthmade via email for comment after regular business hours.
According to the indictment, Lui and his co-conspirators acquired export-controlled computer servers containing advanced GPUs commonly used in artificial intelligence applications.
Prosecutors say the operation relied on a practice known as transshipment, in which goods are routed through intermediate countries before reaching their final destination. U.S. authorities have increasingly focused on such arrangements as companies and individuals seek to evade export restrictions on advanced chips, servers and other technologies subject to national-security controls.
The government alleges the servers could not legally be exported directly to China without special licenses from the Commerce Department.
Instead, prosecutors say the equipment was shipped to countries including Malaysia and Singapore, where export restrictions were less stringent. Once there, the servers were allegedly forwarded to buyers in China.
Investigators also accuse Lui and others of providing U.S. manufacturers with false documentation that concealed the equipment's true destination.
One example cited in court filings involves a January 2024 purchase of 27 servers worth roughly $7.6 million, shipped from Los Angeles to Kuala Lumpur. Prosecutors say a co-conspirator later acknowledged that the servers had been forwarded to a China-based buyer.
The government alleges the broader operation moved more than $300 million worth of restricted technology.
The charges come as the United States continues tightening restrictions on advanced computer chips and AI-related hardware destined for China.
Washington has argued that the most sophisticated semiconductors and computing systems can be used for military, intelligence, and surveillance purposes, making them a national-security concern.
According to prosecutors, the servers involved in the case contained GPUs commonly used in advanced artificial intelligence systems, which the Trump administration now refers to as "Super Intelligence."
Assistant Attorney General John Eisenberg described AI chips as one of the country's most strategically important technologies.
Federal officials allege Lui knowingly circumvented export rules designed to prevent advanced American technology from reaching prohibited users.
The FBI, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, and the Defense Criminal Investigative Service are investigating.
Lui has been charged but not convicted. The allegations are contained in a federal indictment, and he is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.
The federal court docket did not identify legal counsel for Lui, according to Bloomberg .

articles.title_orig: David Jackson wins third World 3D title as France triumph in Yankton
articles.title_zh: David Jackson wins third World 3D title as France triumph in Yankton
articles.content_orig:
France‘s David Jackson took a third World 3D title in barebow men after defeating Spain‘s Cesar Vera Bringas in the final at Yankton 2026 World Archery 3D Championships .
The 34-year-old previously won at the championships in 2019 and 2022, the same year he became world field champion.
The barebow women‘s title also went to France, with Virginie Chevrier triumphing at her maiden world championships, defeating reigning European champion Rosemarie Leitner of Austria.
The compound competition was won by Slovenia‘s Tim Jevsnik , defeating multiply decorated field and 3D champion Nico Wiener of Austria. The reigning European champion, France‘s Aude Ama-Cormerais defeated Ingrid Ronacher , another Austrian former champion, for the women‘s title.
Jackson was also part of France‘s four man men‘s team who also took gold at the event yesterday. The wins pushed France to the top of the medal table for the event, ahead of Austria and Russia.
The traditional bow titles went to Denmark‘s Zibrandt Christensen and Germany‘s Judith Wenzl. The latter is the reigning European champion and Christensen takes his second title after a win in 2017.
The individual longbow competition was won by Russia‘s Mikhail Poddevalin and Austria‘s Johanna Pitschmann , the latter one of the older competitors in the field, winning a world title age 63.
Pitschmann’s victory was perhaps less of a surprise to an unsighted bow field notable for the higher average age of the competitors – in a discipline where experience and learned instinct counts for a great deal.
